title: MONTAGSPECSTROY: Website Development and SEO for a Construction and Engineering Company
case_study_long_title: A Drupal Site for a Construction and Engineering Company

layout.case_study_preview_title: Design, Construction, and Reconstruction

content.text: MONTAGSPECSTROY works across the design, production, construction, and reconstruction of metal structures. Neolines built a Drupal site and wrote it for those stages. No traffic figure is given.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Fabricated steel beams and columns with bolted splice plates in a yard.

content.text: MONTAGSPECSTROY is presented as a construction and engineering company, not as a seller of finished metal goods. The published scope is the design, production, construction, and reconstruction of metal structures for the construction business.

A website capture included with the source adds the firm’s own wording. It says the collective had worked in construction for more than ten years, names a full range of construction-and-installation work, and refers to technologies in construction, installation, and reconstruction. It also mentions European construction technologies and quality standards. The standard is not named, and the “more than ten years” sentence is not dated. Headcount, contract values, and a list of completed buildings are not given.
The engagement length is not stated in the paragraph, so no duration is shown.
A buyer looking for structural design, fabricated steel, installation, or reconstruction is not making one inquiry. A page that only says “metal structures” hides the stage they need.
The work was to put that range on a Drupal site, map the language of construction and metal structures onto the relevant pages, and write for design, construction, and reconstruction.
Named in the case paragraph: design, production, construction, and reconstruction of metal structures.

Named on the website capture, in addition: construction-and-installation work, and a menu that separates Design, Metal structures, and Reconstruction. The same menu also shows a photo album, services, and prices. Those labels are not expanded into a rate card or a project portfolio here.
No drawing set, steel grade, crane plan, or named building is published. The capture is not treated as proof that every menu label was a separately contracted service during the engagement.
Neolines developed the website on Drupal and designed the UX/UI for intuitive use. A theme, a module list, and a screen inventory are not included.

Under the source wordmark the capture prints three lines: design, construction, reconstruction. The visible menu is About, Design, Metal structures, Reconstruction, Photo album, Services, Prices, Feedback, and Contacts. Because the case does not identify that capture as the delivered Drupal site, the menu is evidence of the range the company presented. It is not reconstructed here as the engagement sitemap.

Keyword and competitor analysis was used to build a semantic core and a mapping for an audience in construction and metal structures. The copy was aimed at queries related to design, construction, and reconstruction.
The phrases, the volumes, and the competitor names are not published. Queries named in the MIKS section of the same source page are not part of this case.

layout.case_study_content_title: What Was Not in the Technical List

content.text: The paragraph does not mention page-load work, a mobile audit, or structured data. No schema type is claimed. Promotion is described as a content strategy and website promotion, without an advertising platform or a budget.

Alongside the construction site, the collaboration included a separate website for a charitable foundation supporting children with autism. A review on the source page, written from the point of view of a child-development specialist, describes that work: the site was held to functional and aesthetic standards and made informative for families and caregivers.
The foundation is not named. No count of children, donations, or fundraising result is given. The review is not reprinted here as a client quotation.

The construction company’s own capture has a charity heading and a line that the company supports a children’s fund. That is a statement on the construction site. It is not treated as ownership of the foundation, and it is not one of the engineering services.
The source says the content strategy and website promotion improved visibility in search, attracted targeted traffic, and strengthened recognition and market positioning.
It does not say by how much, over what dates, or from what baseline. No keyword count, lead total, or revenue figure is given. The MIKS percentages on the same page are a different case.
The documented construction work is a Drupal site and an organic-search content program for a firm whose stages run from design and production through construction, installation, and reconstruction.

The charity website is a second project in the same collaboration, kept outside that commercial offer. Company size, a named certificate, a completed building, and a measured traffic result are not claimed.

The photographs of a steel frame, fabricated members, a crane lift, and a reconstruction scene are illustrative. They are not verified MONTAGSPECSTROY contracts. One gallery image is the website capture from the source page. The wireframe photograph illustrates the separate charity website and is not that site.

This is a project and construction practice, not a consumer product line. The relevant outputs are engineered metal structures, their fabrication, their installation, and reconstruction of existing structures. No catalog of retail goods is published.

MONTAGSPECSTROY already worked across design, production, construction, and reconstruction of metal structures. The captured site also describes installation. Those are different stages of one construction practice.
A single metal-products page would collapse that practice into a supplier. Search needed a path for design, for metal structures, for construction and installation, and for reconstruction.

Build the Drupal site, design it for intuitive use, form a semantic core and mapping from keyword and competitor research, and write for design, construction, and reconstruction. A budget and a team size for the engagement are not stated.

A construction or installation search is not filed as a request for a fabricated beam alone.
Reconstruction is named in the paragraph, under the wordmark, and as its own menu item. The capture does not itemize a completed building.
Reconstruction is written as its own stage so it is not absorbed into new-build construction.

Two distinct digital jobs. The commercial one is the Drupal website for the construction company: UX/UI, keyword and competitor research, a semantic core and mapping, and SEO-oriented copy. The other is a separate website for a foundation supporting children with autism, described in a review on the source page.
The foundation is not a construction client and is not described as owned by the company. No advertising account is named for either site.
Drupal is the named platform for the construction site. The information architecture is described as a semantic mapping, not as a published sitemap.

The capture shows Design, Metal structures, and Reconstruction as separate labels, plus About, a photo album, services, prices, feedback, and contacts. That menu is not asserted to be the delivered Drupal tree.
Keyword and competitor analysis produced a semantic core and a mapping for construction and metal-structure searches. Copy subjects named in the paragraph: design, construction, and reconstruction.
No example query is printed. The core’s size is not published.

An integrated copy program for a construction practice, not a visual refresh alone and not a product-catalog campaign. Pages were to carry the terminology of the stage: design, construction, reconstruction, and metal structures.
The source calls the result a content marketing strategy and website promotion. It does not describe a publishing calendar or an ad platform.
The capture has a Feedback item. The case text does not describe a form, a CRM, or a lead count.
This record is a Drupal build, an organic content program, and a separate charity website. It is not an AI-search program.
No answer-engine result is claimed. The capture mentions quality standards and does not name a certificate.

Design, fabrication, installation, and reconstruction are different stages, which is why the mapping matters. The charity website is a different entity and is not placed inside the construction navigation. No city ranking or measured local-search result is published.

Confirmed shape of the construction work: design and build the site on Drupal, with UX/UI aimed at intuitive use; run keyword and competitor analysis; form a semantic core and mapping; write for design, construction, and reconstruction; support the site through content and promotion.
Separately, contribute to a website for a foundation supporting children with autism. Dates for either job are not listed.
Website development on Drupal and UX/UI design for intuitive use. Screens and modules are not listed.
Keyword and competitor analysis, then a semantic core and a mapping for construction and metal structures. Phrases are not published.
Copy for design, construction, and reconstruction, then the content strategy and website promotion the source describes. No traffic figure is attached.
A website for a foundation supporting children with autism, kept outside the construction information architecture. The foundation’s name and any impact figures are not published.

The documented outcome is a Drupal site organized around the stages of a construction and engineering practice, with copy for design, construction, and reconstruction, plus a separate charity website that is not part of that commercial offer.

The source says visibility, targeted traffic, recognition, and positioning improved. It publishes no percentage, no keyword count, no ranking, no leads, and no revenue. Those sentences are not restated here as a measurement. The figures on the MIKS section of the same page are not used.

The useful complexity is a firm that designs, fabricates, installs, and reconstructs, so the website has to name the stage. Treating it as a metal-goods catalog would miss the practice. The charity website is interesting because it is a different kind of site in the same collaboration, and it stays interesting only if it is not folded into the construction services.

title: IVIKOM: Website Development and SEO for a Metal Products Manufacturer
case_study_long_title: A Drupal Site for a Metal Products Manufacturer

layout.case_study_preview_title: Metal Racks, Stands, and Powder Coating

content.text: IVIKOM designs and produces metal products, including racks, advertising stands, cabinets, containers, and powder coating. The published work was a Drupal site, product-focused content, and SEO. No traffic figure is given.

case_study_preview_image.alt: A yellow powder-coated metal storage rack standing in an empty room.

content.text: IVIKOM is a specialized manufacturer of metal products for practical use: metal racks, advertising stands, cabinets, containers, and powder coating. The case presents design and production, not a trading catalog of goods made elsewhere.

A website capture included with the source adds a dated picture of that range. A company note of 21 August 2006 says OOO Ivikom had been making metal products for 11 years, for warehouses, offices, and shops, and that it had its own production space and offices. That sentence is not updated into a current headcount, a floor area, or a founding year.
The engagement brief describes an approximately two-year collaboration. The published paragraph does not give a start date or an end date, so that length is not shown as a closed term.
The offer is several buyer questions at once. A rack, an advertising stand, a cabinet, a container, and a powder-coating job are not the same inquiry.

The work was to put that range on a Drupal site with a semantic core and mapping, and to write the pages in the language of metal products and powder coating, so a visitor and a search engine could tell the lines apart.
Named in the case paragraph: metal racks, advertising stands, cabinets, containers, and powder coating services, inside a practice of designing and producing metal products.

Shown on the website capture, and not itemized in that paragraph: shelving as its own section, tire racks in the gallery, and copy that the racks can be taken apart and moved. The capture’s company note places the products in warehouses, offices, and shops.
No load capacity, dimension, steel grade, or coating standard is published. Advertising stands, cabinets, and containers stay at the level the paragraph gives them.
Neolines developed the website on Drupal and designed the UX/UI for ease of use. That is the platform claim. A theme, a module list, and a set of screens are not included.

The capture’s visible menu is About, Metal products, Shelving, Powder coating, Our work, Feedback, and Contacts. Because the capture carries a 2006 date and the case does not identify it as the delivered Drupal site, that menu is evidence of the range the company presented online. It is not reconstructed here as the engagement sitemap.
During development, keyword and competitor analysis was used to build a semantic core and a mapping aimed at the audience. The source does not publish the phrases, the volumes, or the competitors.
The copy was weighted toward metal-product manufacturing and powder coating. Queries named in the MIKS section of the same source page are not part of this case.

layout.case_study_content_title: What Was Not in the Technical List

content.text: The IVIKOM paragraph does not mention page-load work, a mobile audit, or structured data. Those items appear in the MIKS section and are not copied here. No schema type is claimed.
The source says the content strategy increased visibility, supported promotion in search engines, increased traffic, and improved search results for target queries.

It does not say by how much, over what dates, from what baseline, or to what ranking. No keyword count, lead total, or revenue figure is given. The MIKS percentages on the same page are a different case. This record does not repeat them.
The documented work is a Drupal site and an organic-search content program for a metal-products manufacturer whose named lines are racks, advertising stands, cabinets, containers, and powder coating.
The approximately two-year length comes from the engagement brief. The paragraph itself is undated. Company size, a named certificate, and a measured traffic result are not claimed.

The photographs of racks, tire storage, display stands, a cabinet and container, and a powder-coating booth are illustrative. They are not verified IVIKOM products or photographs of the plant. The last gallery image is the website capture from the source page.

title: MIKS: SEO and Digital Marketing for a Multidisciplinary Industrial Manufacturer
case_study_long_title: A Website Structure for a Multidisciplinary Metal Manufacturer

layout.case_study_preview_title: Structural Steel and a Wider Metal Portfolio

content.text: MIKS manufactures construction metal structures, metal furniture, storage and retail equipment, and installation-related products. The published work organized that range for search and reported the SEO movement below.

case_study_preview_image.alt: A fabricated steel roof truss standing in a fabrication shop.

content.text: MIKS is an industrial manufacturer, not a reseller of finished metal goods. The published range runs from structural metalwork used in substantial construction to metal furniture, storage equipment, retail systems, and products tied to installation.

Structural components of this kind are used in buildings, bridges, and other construction work. The source does not say MIKS constructed those buildings or bridges. Capacity, equipment lists, headcount, and a plant address are not given.
The collaboration is described as spanning two years or more. The published page does not give a start date or an end date, so that length is not shown as a closed term.

The difficulty was the width of the offer. A buyer looking for a beam, a medical metal cabinet, store shelving, or a staircase is not making the same inquiry. One generic metal-products page would hide the line they came for and give search engines a single, vague subject.
The work was to separate those families, write for each one, and keep the plant readable as one manufacturer.

Construction metal structures on the source site: beams, columns, trusses, insert elements, gates and doors, and display stands. Insert elements are kept under that name. They are not expanded into a separate connection-hardware catalog.
Metal furniture and equipment: metal cabinets and workbenches, storage equipment, and medical metal furniture. Electrical enclosures are not named, so they are not added.
Retail and storage: store shelving, and display and dividing stands. The intro also lists retail and storage equipment, industrial cabinets and workbenches, and warehouse and medical furniture.

Construction and installation: staircases, small architectural elements, prefabricated buildings, and waste disposal systems. The intro also lists construction services and mini equipment for municipal and construction applications. The source does not itemize that mini equipment, so no models are added. Prefabricated buildings are a listed product area, not a claim that MIKS delivered complete buildings as a general contractor.

The structure followed the semantic core. Home and About sat above the catalog. About included company history, partners, and certifications. The four catalog families each had dedicated pages for the items above.

That split is what let a navigation label, a category page, and a product description point at the same line. Exact historic URLs are not reconstructed. A platform, a theme, and a module list are not named for this project.

Competitor research was done inside each production area: structural metalwork, storage systems, medical-grade furniture, and custom metal fixtures. The semantic core mixed broader queries with niche ones. The source gives three examples: custom construction beams, medical metal furniture, and industrial shelving.
Those groups were mapped to the pages for the matching line. The size of the core, search volumes, and competitor names are not published.

The technical work covered page-load performance, mobile responsiveness, structured data, and the link structure used for crawling and navigation. A schema type is not named, so none is claimed. No speed score is published.
Each product line was described in the terminology of that line, with phrases aimed at the queries for that line. The catalog was not one plant paragraph repeated under every heading.
A page count and a publishing calendar are not in the source. The certifications page is part of the architecture. The certificates themselves are not named.

Five additional microsites were designed for specific product lines, so those lines could be found on their own rather than only inside the main catalog. The source names construction structures, retail equipment, shelving systems, and furniture.

That is four named lines for five sites. The fifth line is not named. Domains, individual traffic, and rankings for each site are not given. The source does not establish that all five were built from an empty start.

The SEO rows are growth rates, except the keyword row, which is a count. Organic traffic grew 35 percent. Organic sessions grew 20 percent. Total sessions grew 22 percent. Impressions grew 12 percent. Search clicks grew 10 percent. New users grew 40 percent. Returning users grew 30 percent. More than 1,000 additional keywords were indexed.

The keyword count is not a first-page total and not a top-five total. The source does not name the measurement window, the baseline, conversions, leads, or revenue. The closing sentence mentions PPC beside SEO. No platform, budget, or PPC result is given, so none is reported. The click row above is the search-click row, not a paid-click row.

The documented work gave a multidisciplinary metal manufacturer a site that separated structural steelwork, furniture and equipment, retail and storage, and installation-related products, with content and technical SEO written to those lines, plus microsites for selected lines.
The published movement is the SEO rows above. Market leadership, a named certificate, and a completed bridge or building are not claimed.

The photographs are illustrative views of structural steel, a truss, cabinets and a workbench, warehouse racking, retail shelving, and a fabrication floor. They are not verified photographs of the MIKS plant, its employees, or a completed project. The image published with the source case is a website mockup and is not used here.

content.text: AREKS manufactures upholstered furniture and has a showroom on its production site. The published work was the website, competitor analysis, a semantic keyword core, content for each furniture segment, and SEO on Drupal.

case_study_preview_image.alt: A low curved two-seat sofa in dusty rose velvet with slim brass legs.

content.text: AREKS is a family-owned manufacturer of upholstered furniture. The production facility sits in a countryside setting, with a large surrounding area, and the company has its own showroom where customers can view, compare, and select furniture.

The website had to represent that manufacturing business and the showroom’s selection experience. It is not treated here as a general furniture retailer or an online marketplace. The collaboration is remembered as about two years. The source does not give a start date or an end date, so two years is the stated window rather than a verified calendar.

The documented work is website design and development, information architecture, analysis of competitor websites, semantic keyword research, SEO copywriting, ongoing content management, and search-oriented promotion. Development followed Drupal best practices.
A Drupal theme, a module list, a version, advertising platforms, budgets, and performance figures are not stated, so they are not filled in.

The site had to show the furniture collection and still read as a factory with a showroom, not as a catalog with no maker behind it. Visual presentation of upholstery and furniture forms sat next to a structure that let someone move between furniture types.
Interactive configurators, online payment, and delivery services are not in the source, so they are not described as features. The historical implementation used Drupal. No theme or module is named.

The published product list is corner sofas, book-mechanism sofas, eurobook sofas, accordion-mechanism sofas, roll-out sofas, armchairs, and chair beds. Corner sofas are the larger soft configurations. Armchairs and chair beds are listed separately.

Several English labels overlap that list, so they are not added as further categories. Sofa beds, folding sofas, and convertible sofas describe the same mechanisms the source already names. Recliners are not in the AREKS paragraph.

Eurobook is the eurobook fold, not a book. The book mechanism is the other fold, where the seat lifts; it is not a reservation form. Accordion is the accordion fold. Roll-out is the pull-out. No model names were added.

Competing websites were analyzed, and a semantic core was formed around phrases for product type and quality. The source says that work identified distinctive product expressions. Query mapping was then used to tune the content of each segment, rather than one description for the whole collection.
The number of keywords, competitor names, search volumes, ranking positions, and traffic changes are not published, so none are added.
Copy and ongoing content management supported both navigation and organic search. Category content was written for the furniture type on that page.
A publishing schedule and a page count are not in the source, so they are not stated.
The source describes an integrated approach: design, development, copywriting, and SEO, taking Drupal practice into account. That is the documented promotion.
A named advertising platform, a budget, click volume, conversions, a campaign structure, and return on ad spend are not published. House of Sofas figures are not used here.

Website development, a product architecture built from the published furniture types, competitor analysis, semantic mapping, content management, and Drupal-based SEO practice supported the digital presence of a family-owned upholstered furniture manufacturer with its own showroom.
No ranking, traffic, or sales figure is attached. Market leadership and a guaranteed result are not claimed.

title: House of Sofas: SEO, PPC and Website Development for a Sofa Manufacturer
case_study_long_title: Growing Online Visibility for a Sofa Manufacturing Business

layout.case_study_preview_title: A Sofa Manufacturer with Its Own Showroom

content.text: House of Sofas manufactures sofas and sells them from its own showroom. The published work covered the website, a catalog of sofa types and folding mechanisms, technical and on-page SEO, category and blog content, and paid search with seven ad groups and around 45 ads.

case_study_preview_image.alt: A compact two-seat sofa in sand boucle with rounded arms and thin black legs.

content.text: House of Sofas is a sofa manufacturer with its own showroom and sales operation. The collection covers more than one sofa type and more than one folding mechanism, and customers could see products in person as well as on the site.

The website had to represent that manufacturing business and still help someone find the showroom, see a promotion, and compare models. It is not treated here as a general furniture retailer, a marketplace, or a reseller. The published source describes a two-year collaboration. It does not give a start date or an end date, so two years is the stated window rather than a verified calendar.

The documented work is website development, SEO strategy and keyword research, the information architecture, technical and on-page SEO, product-category content, informational blog content, ongoing content support, and PPC management.
Project dates inside that two-year window, campaign budgets, a named advertising platform, and a programming stack are not stated, so they are not filled in.

The navigation was kept short: home, about, promotions, the product catalog, a blog, and contact. That put the catalog, the showroom details, current promotions, and a way to inquire within one structure instead of a long product menu at the top.

Inside the catalog, the published categories are sectional sofas, sofa beds, ottomans, sofas, eurobook sofas, book-mechanism sofas, dolphin-mechanism sofas, click-clack sofas, pull-out sofas, accordion-mechanism sofas, and recliner chairs. Sectional sofas are the larger configurations, including the corner-sofa queries named in the research. Couches and sofas appear as two labels in the source and are one general sofa category here.

A few source labels are mechanisms, not themes. Eurobook is the eurobook fold, not a book. The book mechanism is the other fold, where the seat lifts; it is not a reservation form. Dolphin is the dolphin pull-out bed mechanism, not a themed product. Click-clack, pull-out, and accordion stay as their own categories because the source lists them separately. No model names were added.

Technical work named in the source covered page-load performance, structured data, and mobile presentation, alongside a structure search engines could crawl by category. Category pages were optimized around the product each page actually sold.
No performance score, schema type, Core Web Vitals figure, or mobile ranking change is published, so none is added.

Keyword and competitor research set the map for the catalog. Named examples include sectional sofa, sofa bed, eurobook sofa, and recliner chairs, and longer queries such as modern sofa bed, reclining sectional sofa, and affordable corner sofa. Category copy used the terms that matched that page, including higher-intent product queries, rather than one description repeated across the range.

The blog carried professional advice, product information, and sofa care. The source also describes explanations of materials, comfort-related features, and maintenance. Those subjects are the content strategy. Article titles, studies, and technical claims that are not in the source are not invented. Product pages and informational pages together covered someone choosing a mechanism and someone learning how to look after a sofa.
Paid search sat beside the organic catalog. The source describes seven ad groups and around 45 targeted advertisements. That is a group structure, not seven separate campaigns, and 45 is approximate.

Ad messages addressed different stages of the buying journey and the points the source actually names: showroom access, product variety, and promotions. Campaigns were monitored, with adjustments to bids and audience targeting. The platform, the budget, return on ad spend, and a lead count are not published.

The figures below are the published source results. They are not a new analytics audit. Organic traffic and organic visits are separate rows. The visit row is the source’s organic-sessions figure. The keyword figure is an increase of 950 keywords in Google rankings: a count of additional keywords with improved positions, not a claim that all 950 reached the first page or the top five. Top-five keyword performance is a separate +30 percent, and the source does not define that measure. PPC conversion growth and conversion-rate growth are also separate, and a conversion is not defined as a completed sofa sale.
Organic traffic: +35%
Organic visits: +12%
Total sessions: +16%
Keyword visibility: 950 additional keywords with improved Google search positions
Top-five keyword performance: +30%
Impressions: +8%
Clicks: +7%

Returning visits: +20%
PPC clicks: +25%
PPC conversions: +95%

None of these percentages is converted into an absolute total. A measurement period inside the two-year window, a baseline, an attribution model, and an advertising budget are not stated.
Website structure, technical and on-page SEO, product-focused content, and PPC optimization strengthened House of Sofas’ search visibility and the reported conversion performance.

The source says this supported the company’s presence in more than one city and supported sales growth. Cities are not named, and no revenue figure is attached to the campaigns. Market leadership and a guaranteed result are not claimed.

title: Siblux: SEO and PPC for Timber Houses and Premium Wooden Windows

layout.case_study_preview_title: Timber Houses and Premium Wooden Windows

content.text: Siblux designs, produces, and builds glued-laminated timber houses, and it also designs and manufactures premium wooden windows and insulated glazing, including installation on larger buildings. The published work gave those two lines a clearer website structure, section-level SEO content, a later redesign, and paid search beside organic visibility.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Close view of a timber-house facade with divided wooden window frames and horizontal wood siding.

content.text: Siblux is a manufacturer and construction company with two connected lines of work. One is the design, production, and construction of glued-laminated timber houses, taken through the project cycle. The other is the design and manufacture of premium wooden windows and insulated glazing units, including installation.

Those lines are not the same offer. A house project and a window system answer different questions, and window installation is not described as residential only. The company also took part in exhibitions and operated showrooms in major cities. Awards and certifications are mentioned in the source overview without the documents being named, so none are listed here. A collaboration length is not stated on this record, so none is published. The source does say the first website design was followed by a redesign about two years later.
The practical problem was presentation. Complete timber-house projects and premium wooden window systems are technically different, and the site had to make that difference obvious.

Visitors also needed a logical way through products, projects, properties, exhibitions, and the rest of the company information. This case does not add competitor findings, unnamed business problems, or client quotations that are not in the source.
The structure grouped the company’s own products and services first, then kept examples and company information beside them rather than inside them.

On the house side, the published areas covered timber houses, glued-laminated timber houses, and glued-laminated timber as a material. On the window side, they covered wooden window design, double-glazed window units, window manufacturing, installation, materials, and hardware. A person looking for a house did not have to pass through a window page to get there, and the reverse was also true.

Projects, properties and completed buildings, exhibitions, a blog, contact, company advantages, and galleries were supporting destinations. That split is what made the navigation more logical: a product page explains what is made, a project or property page shows completed work, and the remaining pages explain the company. Exact historic URLs are not reconstructed.

SEO copy was written for the individual sections, using the semantic keyword research and the information architecture as the map. The aim was alignment: the intent of the query, the job of the page, and the terms on that page had to agree.

House content explained the benefits of glued-laminated timber and the house project itself. Window content explained wooden window design and manufacturing, including insulated glazing. Supporting pages carried both business directions without folding them into one generic article. No ranking position is added here beyond the figures in Results.
The site first received a design shaped around the business and that content structure. About two years later, a redesign was carried out to improve usability and the visual presentation.

The historic site used Drupal, HTML, CSS, and PHP. That is the implementation stack of the project being described. It is not a claim about the company’s current stack, and it is not this Next.js and Payload site. The source describes that Drupal build as functional and responsive. This case study does not add a separate responsive audit.

Organic search and paid search were used together for both lines: timber houses, and premium wooden windows. SEO carried the structure and the section content. Paid search was aimed at the same demand, so a query could meet either an organic page or an ad without the two programmes describing different companies.

The useful reading is search visibility, relevant traffic, advertising efficiency, and conversion performance. The platform is not named. Campaign budgets, lead counts, revenue, and return on ad spend are not in the source, so they are not estimated.

The figures below are the published source results. They are not a new analytics audit. Organic traffic and organic sessions are separate rows. The keyword figure is a count of additional keywords with improved Google positions, not a percentage and not a count of top-five rankings. Top-five keyword performance is a separate +40 percent, and the source does not say whether that change is position, clicks, or another measure.

Organic sessions: +25%
Total sessions: +30%
Keyword visibility: more than 800 additional keywords with improved Google search positions
Top-five keyword performance: +40%
Impressions: +15%

Structured website content, SEO, a redesign about two years after the first design, and PPC together strengthened Siblux’s search visibility and brought a broader audience to two different offers: glued-laminated timber houses, and premium wooden windows.
That is as far as the source goes. Market leadership, a guaranteed result, and revenue growth are not claimed.

content.text: The published source describes Geotermal as an e-commerce platform for heating equipment and installation systems, from boilers and pumps to radiators and water heaters, for residential and commercial buildings. This case uses the English name Geothermal. The source spelling is Geotermal.

The distinction that had to survive on the website is the complete system. Categories named in the source are boilers, heat pumps, radiators, water heaters, and complete heating systems, plus professional installation. Third-party brands stay third-party. Manufacturer names are not listed in the source paragraph, so they are not invented.

A boiler, a heat pump, a circulation pump, a radiator, and a water heater are separate purchases. They only heat a building if pipework, distribution, controls, and the plant layout match the equipment. The site had to show that relationship without turning every component into one generic “heating” page.

Capacities, pipe dimensions, certifications, and safety guarantees are not published and are not added here. Gas-fired and other fuel-fired equipment still needs the design and installation that the equipment type requires. This page does not substitute for that requirement.

The documented service is professional installation of complete heating systems, alongside the catalog. A useful public explanation of that work covers the building and its heat demand, the choice of equipment, the plant layout, distribution through the building, installation, and making the system ready to run.

That sequence is how the subject has to be explained. It is not a published Geothermal method statement. Ongoing maintenance, seasonal preparation, response times, and a service contract are not in the source, so they are not claimed. Documented building contexts are residential and commercial. Hotels and apartment buildings are not named as customers.
The original site was developed on Drupal with custom HTML, CSS, and PHP. That is the historic store. It is not a claim that the current Next.js and Payload site is that implementation.

The published structure organized boilers, heat pumps, radiators, water heaters, and complete heating systems so navigation, brand pages, product comparisons, and installation information could sit beside one another. Exact historic URLs and interface details that are not in the source are not reconstructed.

Mapping put those terms on category, brand, and service pages, with internal links between a product and the complete-system destination.
The 2,000 figure is the size of the core. The source says the work improved search visibility, organic traffic, and conversions. It does not publish the percentages, so none are added.

PPC campaigns sat beside SEO for product sales and installation-related services. The useful split is intent: a specific piece of equipment versus a complete system for a building, with the landing page matching that query.
The source does not name the advertising platform, the number of campaigns, or the budgets. Those details are not borrowed from another case.

layout.case_study_preview_title: Materials, Heating, and a Complete Sauna or Bath

content.text: Sauna Shop is a specialized e-commerce and construction-solutions business for designing and building saunas and Russian baths — materials, heaters, chimneys, and interior finishing — not only a storefront for stoves and accessories. Over approximately two years Neolines built the semantic architecture, Drupal site, content, and contextual advertising around both a single product purchase and a complete room.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Dark wood sauna with lit tiered benches, a glass door, and a compact heater topped with stones.

content.text: The published source describes Sauna Shop as a niche e-commerce platform for construction materials, stoves, and accessories used to build bespoke saunas and steam rooms. The historic storefront also offered wood-fired and electric heaters, stainless chimney systems, timber, doors, stones, and interior finishing of the steam room.

The point of the site was that those pieces belonged together. A buyer could take one accessory or plan the room. Third-party stove brands in the catalog are manufacturers represented in the store, not Sauna Shop factories. Russian bath names the type of room, not a geographic market.

The collaboration is recorded as approximately two years, covering keyword research, website architecture, content, Drupal design and development, and contextual advertising. The published Sauna Shop paragraph does not print a start date or an end date, and the window is not a verified month-by-month campaign log.
Not every catalog branch is claimed for every month of those two years. The source describes an evolving site: categories and the keyword base were revised as the range developed.

The documented structure served two intents at once: buying one product, and assembling a sauna or bath. Main catalog branches included stoves for baths and saunas — wood-fired, electric, accessories, and controls — stainless chimney systems, timber, doors, interior finishing, sauna stones, and related accessories such as facing materials.
Service paths covered payment, delivery, the cart, and contacts. Insulation is named in the published project description alongside timber and accessories. Exact historic URLs are not reconstructed.

layout.case_study_content_title: From a Single Product to a Finished Room

content.text: A complete room, as far as the sources support it, meant planning the space, choosing timber and insulation, selecting a wood-fired or electric heater, matching a chimney, allowing for ventilation, and finishing the interior. The historic storefront described specialist consultation on the stove, on construction materials, and on interior finishing of the steam room.
That is a construction solution built from a catalog and finishing work. It is not a published engineering standard, a structural package, or a safety guarantee.

The documented SEO work began with keyword and competitor research in sauna and bath construction. A semantic core of approximately 1,500 optimized keywords was mapped onto categories and subcategories, from heaters to timber, insulation, and accessories, with internal linking between those destinations.

Product descriptions and educational copy covered both purchase intent and planning intent. The 1,500 figure is the size of that core. The source describes sustained growth in organic traffic, visibility, and conversions, and it does not publish the percentages. Rankings by query are not reconstructed.

The original site was developed on Drupal with custom HTML, CSS, and PHP. That is historical context for the Sauna Shop store. It is not a claim that the current Next.js and Payload site is that implementation.

The published design goal was a catalog people could actually use: clear category navigation, product information, and educational content. Interface details that are not in the source are not invented.

Digital promotion sat beside the organic programme so product and construction queries could reach a relevant landing page: a stove, a material category, a chimney, or an accessory. The split followed search intent rather than one generic offer.
The Sauna Shop source does not name the advertising platform, the number of campaigns, budgets, or paid results. Those figures are not borrowed from any other case.

The historic storefront showed third-party brands including Harvia, Feringer, Kastor, Termofor, Vesuvius, Varvara, Teplov i Sukhov, Talc, and Doorwood. They are manufacturers and suppliers in the catalog.
Sauna Shop is not described as the maker of those products. Additional brand names are not added.
A sauna catalog only works when the stove, the flue, the timber, and the finishing can be found as separate destinations and still read as one room.

layout.case_study_preview_title: Heating, Sauna, Fireplace, and Chimney Solutions

content.text: Stove Shop is a heating, sauna, fireplace, and building-solutions business: an e-commerce catalog of more than 3,000 models and 40-plus brands, plus metal-chimney production and stove and boiler installation — not merely a storefront selling stoves. Over approximately seven years Neolines combined ongoing SEO, Google Ads, Google Merchant Center product feeds, website architecture, and content as product ranges and service pages evolved.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Wood-fired sauna stove with a stone cage installed in a timber bath interior beside cedar benches.

content.text: The published source describes Stove Shop as a comprehensive online store for heating stoves, sauna stoves, fireplaces, boilers, chimney systems, and accessories, with more than 3,000 listed models and more than 40 brands. The same record names production and installation of metal chimneys, and stove and boiler installations.

Those figures are historical project information from the source. They are not a live stock count. Third-party brand names in the catalog are manufacturers represented in the store, not Stove Shop factories.

Neolines collaborated with Stove Shop for seven years. That figure is the published relationship and the window for the SEO and PPC report. It is not a verified month-by-month campaign log, and no start or end date is assigned.

The work is described as continuous refinement of SEO and PPC around high-demand keywords and a diverse brand portfolio, together with website structure, content, and design updates as the range evolved. Not every service listed on the later site is claimed for every year of the seven.

The documented information architecture aligned a large catalog with the semantic core. Main categories were Stoves, Boilers, and Chimneys. Stove types included Russian bath stoves, sauna stoves, fireplace stoves, heating stoves, fireboxes, and accessories. Chimney sets split indoor systems, outdoor systems, and components.

Company and service pages covered the shopping cart, contacts, reviews, delivery, a price list, and installation services. A Russian-bath section covered ventilation, choosing a bath stove, and bath-design aspects — a bathing-facility type, not a geographic market. An FAQ captured recurring product and kit questions. Exact historic URLs and the CMS are not reconstructed.
More than 40 brands were represented. Names published on the source page include Feringer, META, Breneran, Vulcan, Harvia, Teplodar, Jotul, Invicta, Kratki, Nordica, Romotop, Tim Sistem, and Eurokom.

Dedicated brand content covered product features, comparisons, and installation instructions so searchers who used a manufacturer name could land on a relevant page. Those manufacturers remain third-party brands. Additional names are not added.

The documented SEO work started with keyword and competitor research spanning heating stoves, sauna stoves, fireplace inserts, and chimney kits, producing a semantic core of roughly 3,000 keywords. That core was mapped onto categories, subcategories, brand pages, and service pages.

Over seven years the keyword base and site structure were revised as ranges changed. On-page work, category optimisation, educational content, FAQ, internal navigation, and seasonal targeting for sauna stoves, heating equipment, fireplaces, and chimney systems are named as part of that process. Rankings by query are not reconstructed.

title: Grosstek: Digital Marketing and SEO for an ACP Manufacturer
case_study_long_title: Grosstek — Two-Year SEO, Drupal Website Architecture and Contextual Advertising for In-House Aluminum Composite Panel Manufacturing

layout.case_study_preview_title: In-House Aluminum Composite Panel Manufacturing

content.text: Grosstek is a large-scale manufacturer and installer of aluminum composite facade panels, with its own production lines and product brands Grosbond and Konstruktor — not a distributor that only buys finished sheets and cuts them to size. Over approximately two years Neolines combined Drupal website architecture, visual design, SEO and contextual advertising, working through the product lines, manufacturing information, applications, documentation, portfolio and inquiry paths with company management.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Large contemporary commercial tower with a champagne and graphite aluminum composite cassette facade.

content.text: The published source describes Grosstek as a large-scale manufacturer and installer specialising in aluminum composite panels for building facades. The digital project was to give that factory a usable online presence: SEO, a highly targeted PPC programme, website development and content optimisation.

The distinction that had to survive on the website is manufacturing. Grosstek runs production. Grosbond and Konstruktor are its product lines. Associated engineering, mounting systems, fastening components and installation sit beside that factory, as do architectural applications that may include glass or natural stone. Those applications are not treated here as extra in-house panel brands.

Neolines collaborated with Grosstek for over two years. That figure is the published relationship and the window for the SEO and PPC report. It is not a verified month-by-month campaign log, and no start or end date is assigned.

Website structure and design were discussed in depth with company management and managers responsible for different areas of the business: how to organise product lines, manufacturing information, applications, technical documentation, the project portfolio and commercial inquiries. Names, attendee counts and meeting dates are not disclosed.

The site was developed on Drupal. The published information architecture included a homepage; About Us (history, news, partners, certifications); Ventilated Facades (advantages, installation and construction); product lines Grosbond and Konstruktor, each with application, processing, storage and certification sections; a production-process overview; completed-project case studies; a Press Center for news and industry insights; and contact / inquiry paths for professional buyers.

A new website design balanced a functional interface with a warm colour palette and professional imagery. That is documented visual-identity work for a manufacturing brand. The authentic Grosstek mark from the published source case page is used in this record. No Grosstek, Grosbond or Konstruktor mark was generated.

The documented information architecture organised the Drupal site around eight hubs that assembled a shared main page through section interfaces: Company, Ventilated Facades, Grosbond, Konstruktor, Facade systems, Production, Products and Objects, with a Press Center feeding the same homepage.

Company covered about, history, news, reviews, partners, certificates and contacts. Ventilated Facades covered application, purpose, advantages, composite panels, substructures, design, installation and supervised installation. Grosbond and Konstruktor each held composite-panel pages for application, advantages, colour, characteristics, production, processing, storage, certificates, prices and request.

Facade systems listed application, purpose, features, production, certificates, prices and request, and named associated applications as labelled on the project diagram, including keramogranite — not additional in-house panel brands. Production listed technology, chemical synthesis, coating, thermo-adhesive, painting, processing and control. Products grouped Grosbond, Konstruktor and subsystem pages. Objects held the project portfolio. The Press Center held promotions, special offers, news, articles, questions, reviews, blog, experts, photo and video.
Editorial and promotional content sat under the relevant hubs. Exact historic URLs are not reconstructed. The diagram below is the authentic project website structure.

media.alt: Grosstek website information architecture diagram with Company, Ventilated Facades, Grosbond, Konstruktor, Facade systems, Production, Products, Objects and Press Center hubs feeding section interfaces and the main page.

content.text: Grosbond and Konstruktor needed destinations that could hold application, processing, storage and certification information without flattening them into one “composite panels” page. Exact certificate names and datasheets are not reconstructed.

Production was treated as a differentiator. The documented process outline runs from thermosetting and chemical synthesis through painting and final quality checks. That outline structures the manufacturing content. It is not expanded here into an invented factory recipe. Line speeds, plant locations and capacity are not disclosed.

Aluminum composite panels sit on substructures with fastening systems; design and installation have to match that cassette. The source names turnkey facade services as part of how Grosstek differentiated itself in competitor research, and it names a projects section covering scope, materials and outcomes.

No project names, dimensions or cities are listed in the extract used here, so none are invented. Glass and natural stone, where they appear, are architectural applications in a wider facade portfolio — not Grosstek-manufactured equivalents of Grosbond. Inquiry paths for construction companies, architects, developers and project managers used the existing contact and form pattern. No new form was added for this Case Study.

The documented SEO work is in-depth keyword research and competitor benchmarking in aluminum composite panels and facade systems, including terms such as ventilated facades, composite panels and facade construction solutions, grouped by intent and volume.

A semantic core clustered themes such as Grosbond panel technology, industrial facade systems and aluminum panel installation. Content mapping assigned each cluster to a page so product, production and installation copy would not overlap. On-page work included unique technical content, meta titles and descriptions, and schema markup for Product and Service pages. Competitor brands from the analysis are not named.

PPC sat beside the organic programme. The source describes about ten targeted ad groups — including industrial facade systems, composite-panel wholesale and turnkey facade installations — with more than fifty ads and landing pages aligned to the ad copy.

content.text: PromTehMontg designs, prepares and installs ventilated facade systems as an integrated offering: engineering, processing of cladding materials, mounting-system design, fastening components, and installation. Neolines supported that business with keyword and competitor research, a semantic core clustered around services and materials, website structure, and search-oriented content for relevant service and material pages — not a generic facade-benefits brochure, and not a results table that the source does not publish.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Modern metal-and-glass facade with horizontal panel bands, photographed looking up in daylight.

content.text: PromTehMontg is a facade engineering and installation company, not only a site crew hanging one cladding type. The published source describes a ventilated-facade installation business with a complete SEO programme, content mapping, and a website organised around services, materials and technical expertise, with custom design aligned to professional branding.

The operating model that had to be represented is wider than that paragraph: design, preparation and processing of materials, mounting-system engineering, supply of fastening components, and installation across several ventilated-facade cladding types. This case is about that digital work. It is not a primer on rainscreen physics, and Neolines did not install the facades.
The documented product and service navigation included these cladding types and systems:
Aluminum composite panels
Ceramic-magnesite facade boards
Aluminum facade cassettes
Natural stone cladding
Galvanized steel facade cassettes
Brick-effect facade panels
Facade substructures and mounting systems designed for these different cladding materials
Engineering, preparation, processing, and installation of facade systems

Different skins need different supporting structures. Weight, format, joint and movement change the subframe. That is why mounting-system engineering belongs beside the material list, not as a footnote under a finished photograph.

Material names are kept as supplied. Brick-effect panels are not treated as fired brick. Ceramic-magnesite boards are not rewritten as fibre cement. Specifications, fire ratings, certifications and energy-efficiency claims are not added.

A professional buyer may need an ACP cassette, a stone rainscreen, a ceramic-magnesite board, a galvanized steel cassette, a brick-effect panel, a mounting profile, an engineering package or a turnkey crew. Those intents are connected. They are not the same page.

The website had to organise that range so construction companies, developers, contractors and architects could find a relevant solution without flattening the offering into generic facade advantages. No historic domain, previous CMS or complaint log is recorded.

The documented work is a complete SEO strategy: in-depth keyword research, competitor analysis, a semantic core, structured content mapping, and optimisation of service and material pages. Search intent was clustered around individual facade materials, cassette systems, panel types, mounting subsystems, engineering and installation — so the copy could follow the actual navigation of the business.

That is a description of method. It is not a claim that every material had a verified standalone URL. A keyword count is not published for PromTehMontg and is not borrowed from AluMatrix. Rankings are mentioned qualitatively on the source page and are not converted into a table.

The published site structure guided visitors through services, materials and technical expertise. Unique, search-oriented content was prepared for relevant service and material categories. Custom design supported professional branding rather than treating the project as a visual redesign alone.

A logical industrial website holds engineering, processing, mounting and installation next to the cladding types it actually works with. Historic URLs, CMS name and a reconstructed sitemap are not disclosed.

Industrial B2B marketing for a facade engineer-installer works when the website matches the operating model: several cladding materials, the subsystems that carry them, and the engineering and installation that make them a building envelope.

Semantic research, content planning and navigation only pay off if they follow that range. Where the source is silent — traffic, rankings, duration, named sites, datasheets — the correct public line is Not disclosed.

items.question: What does an integrated ventilated facade solution include?

content.text: In this record, an integrated solution can include facade engineering and design, preparation and processing of cladding materials, mounting-system engineering, supply of fastening components, and installation of the ventilated envelope.

That is the operating model. It is not a claim that every job included every stage, or that PromTehMontg manufactures every cladding brand in-house. Named buildings and specifications are not disclosed.

items.question: Why do different facade cladding materials need different mounting subsystems?

content.text: Cladding weight, format, joint type and movement differ. Aluminum composite panels and aluminum cassettes, ceramic-magnesite boards, natural stone, galvanized steel cassettes and brick-effect panels do not share one default subframe. The supporting structure has to match the skin: load path, ventilation gap, and how the panel is fixed.

That is general facade-engineering practice. PromTehMontg’s documented work includes mounting systems designed for these different cladding materials. Load tables, spans and coatings are not published.

items.question: What is the difference between aluminum composite panels, facade cassettes, and brick-effect panels?

content.text: Aluminum composite panels are sheet products with aluminum faces used as rainscreen cladding. Aluminum and galvanized steel facade cassettes are folded metal units. Brick-effect facade panels imitate brick coursing; they are not treated here as fired masonry. Ceramic-magnesite facade boards are a separate board product and are not renamed as stone or fibre cement.
These are category descriptions for search and navigation. They are not PromTehMontg product datasheets.

title: VentFasad: SEO and Website Strategy for Facade Installation
case_study_long_title: VentFasad — Keyword Research, Semantic Architecture, Content Management and Custom Website Design for Ventilated Facade Installation

layout.case_study_preview_title: Ventilated Facade Installation and Building-Envelope Contracting

content.text: VentFasad is a facade-installation contractor working with ventilated facade systems, engineering, mounting components and building-envelope projects. Over approximately one year, Neolines combined keyword research, competitor analysis, a targeted semantic core, content mapping, SEO-oriented information architecture, custom facade-industry website design, and content management so those connected services could be found and understood by professional buyers.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Large civic office building with a terracotta and sand ventilated cassette facade and visible panel joints.

content.text: VentFasad installs ventilated facade systems and delivers related building-envelope work: facade project planning and engineering, fabrication of mounting and fastening components, and cladding installation as an integrated contractor service on commercial and other buildings.

This case is about the digital work beside that contracting business — not a primer on rainscreens, and not a claim that Neolines installed the facades. Named sites, employee counts and certifications are not disclosed.

A specialized facade contractor has to show several connected capabilities at once: the visible cladding, the mounting subsystem, the engineering, and the installation. Construction companies, developers, architects, engineers and commercial-property stakeholders typically search those jobs separately. That is a sector observation, not a verified VentFasad customer list.
The website had to distinguish those services without inventing a complaint the source does not record. No historic domain or previous CMS is named.

The documented SEO work is in-depth keyword research, competitor analysis, and a targeted semantic core covering high-, mid- and low-frequency queries around ventilated-facade installation. Search terms were grouped so content mapping could assign clusters to pages rather than dumping every query onto a contractor homepage.

That map informed the information architecture, on-page headings, meta descriptions, internal linking and image alt text. The source does not publish a keyword count for VentFasad. The 2,000-term core belongs to the related AluMatrix engagement, not this record.

Content planning kept each page attached to a real service or intent: installation, engineering, mounting, facade type. Unique technical copy described processes and installation practice, with keywords placed in headings, lists and alt attributes.

Content management, in this engagement, is the discipline of keeping that map consistent after the site is designed — so the copy still matches what the contractor actually does. No article count or editorial calendar is published.

A custom website was designed for the facade industry, with intuitive navigation and a structure built for both SEO and usability. Design, content structure and search architecture were treated as one system: the navigation had to express the semantic map, not fight it.
Theme, CMS, responsive-framework names and a reconstructed sitemap are not disclosed. No conversion-rate improvement is published for the design itself.

The working relationship lasted approximately one year. In that window the project combined SEO preparation, content management and website design. That duration is the cooperation period. It is not a dated campaign log, and it is not converted here into rankings, leads or revenue.

The work is described as successful through that coherence — a contractor site that could present engineering, mounting and installation as related jobs — not through invented statistics. A Russian source passage that attributes “leading positions” and conversion growth without figures, and that even names AluMatrix in the VentFasad result, is not used as a metrics table.

Facade installation marketing fails when the site only shows finished buildings. Professional buyers also search for the subframe, the engineering and the contracting service. Keyword research, content mapping and website architecture have to be planned together so those jobs have destinations.
Where the source is silent — traffic, rankings, CMS, named buildings — the correct public line is Not disclosed.

items.question: What is a ventilated facade system?

content.text: A ventilated facade, or rainscreen, is a cladding system in which panels sit on a mounting subframe with an air gap behind them. The visible skin, the subframe and the insulation work together. That is general construction practice, not a VentFasad product specification.
VentFasad’s documented work is planning, engineering, mounting-component fabrication and installation of such systems. Panel brands, spans and U-values are not disclosed.

items.question: What role do mounting and fastening components play in facade installation?

content.text: The panel only performs if it is fixed correctly. Rails, brackets and fasteners carry load, create the ventilation gap and absorb movement. VentFasad’s scope includes fabrication of mounting and fastening components as well as installation.
Bracket catalogues, load tables and coatings are not in the source.

items.question: What should a building owner or contractor consider when selecting a facade installation company?

content.text: Whether the contractor can connect engineering, the mounting subsystem and on-site installation, and whether the website describes those jobs separately enough to be found. Typical audiences in this sector include construction companies, developers, architects and engineers. That is a market observation, not a VentFasad client list.
Certifications, warranties and named contracts are not published for this record.

layout.case_study_preview_title: Aluminum Composite Panels and Ventilated Facade Systems

content.text: AluMatrix designs, manufactures and sells aluminum composite panels and mounting subsystems for commercial and industrial ventilated facades. Neolines supported that manufacturing business with a semantic core of more than 2,000 keywords, technical content and schema, a blog for long-tail facade queries, and contextual advertising structured as three PPC campaigns. The published source reports SEO, paid-search and social figures after two years of collaboration.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Modern commercial building clad in silver-grey aluminum composite panels with visible ventilated-facade joints.

content.text: AluMatrix — published on the source page as Alumatrix — operates in facade systems and building materials. The confirmed offering is the design, manufacturing and sale of aluminum composite panels and mounting subsystems, with customised ventilated facades in a range of colours and configurations, plus installation using fastening systems.

Production and processing cover coating, thermal bonding, painting and quality control. That is a manufacturing and construction-materials business, not a generic cladding reseller. Stone facades and glass curtain-wall systems are not documented in the source and are not added here.

A technically broad facade offering is easy to flatten online. Professional buyers may search by material (aluminum composite panels), by system (ventilated facades), by component (mounting and fastening), by process (coating, painting) or by service (installation).

Those intents are related. They are not the same page. The marketing job was to present the manufacturing, engineering and installation capability so construction companies, architects and specifiers could find the right destination. No historic domain, previous CMS or customer complaint is recorded, so none is invented.

The documented SEO work started with competitor analysis in industrial and construction search, then a semantic core of over 2,000 keywords covering aluminum composite panels, ventilated facades and installation systems across stages of the buyer journey.

That core was mapped onto site sections for ventilated facades (benefits, types, applications, structural details), AluMatrix panels (descriptions, colours, processing options) and manufacturing (technologies, coating, thermal bonding, painting, quality control). Unique technical copy, optimised titles, meta descriptions and image alt text supported those pages. A blog captured long-tail queries around technical insights, installation guidelines and facade-industry trends. Schema markup and a link-building campaign aimed at industry sites and forums are also named.

The same source page documents related ventilated-facade SEO work for VentFasad, GPTM GROUP, PromTehMontg, Facade Installation and Grosstek. Those are separate engagements. They are not AluMatrix brands. They illustrate that a facade semantic foundation can be adapted; they are not additional AluMatrix factories.

The documented information architecture organised the AluMatrix website around six hubs that assembled a shared main page: Company, Ventilated Facades, AluMatrix product pages, Production, Services, and a Press Center.

Company pages covered about, history, news, reviews, partners, certificates and contacts. Ventilated facades covered purpose, types, design, advantages, systems, technical specifications, engineering and installation. The AluMatrix product branch covered composite panels, applications, colour, characteristics, production, processing, certificates and prices. Production listed factory stages including technology, chemical synthesis, coating, thermal bonding, painting, processing and quality control, plus a scientific department as labelled on the diagram. Services covered design, processing, installation, manufacturing, installation supervision and logistics.

Each product and production hub had a section interface of related pages. Editorial and promotional content — news, articles, questions, reviews, blog, experts, photos, videos, promotions and special offers — sat under the relevant hubs and the Press Center. Exact historic URLs and the CMS are not reconstructed. The diagram below is the project website structure.

items.question: What are aluminum composite panels used for in facade construction?

content.text: The source describes aluminum composite panels as multilayer sheets — two aluminum faces with a polyethylene or mineral core — used in facade systems, and also in interior finishes and signage.

AluMatrix designs, manufactures and sells those panels in a range of colours and configurations for commercial and industrial ventilated facades. Exact thicknesses, fire classes and warranties are not republished here as a catalogue.

items.question: How do ventilated facade systems differ from other facade solutions?

content.text: A ventilated facade is a rainscreen: panels sit on a mounting subsystem with an air gap, rather than being bonded as a solid skin. That is why the source treats ventilated facades as their own section — benefits, types, applications and structural details — instead of folding them into a generic cladding page.
Stone and glass curtain-wall systems are not documented as AluMatrix offerings in this record.

items.question: Why are mounting and fastening systems important in facade installation?

content.text: The panel only performs if it is fixed correctly. AluMatrix supplies mounting subsystems as well as panels, and the source FAQ describes installation with fastening systems, geometry control and attention to environmental and architectural conditions.
Bracket models, span tables and load calculations are not in the source.

content.text: Aleks SF designs, engineers, manufactures and installs custom retail furniture for jewelry stores — display cabinets, glass showcases, pedestals and complete salon interiors. Neolines supported that manufacturing business with a Drupal website, a semantic SEO foundation of about 1,000 keywords, ongoing search promotion and contextual advertising. The published source describes a decade-long partnership; organic results are reported over an eight-year window.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Bright jewelry salon with white glass-top counters, island vitrines and a tall display cabinet.

content.text: Aleks SF is a B2B manufacturer of custom retail equipment for jewelry boutiques. The physical offering is a complete service cycle: conceptual design, engineering, production of display cabinets and pedestals with glass doors and showcases, and on-site installation in jewelry stores.

That is the core of the case. The digital work existed to present that offering to business customers and to keep it visible in search. Neolines did not manufacture the furniture and did not install the salons. Aleks SF did.

A specialized store-fitting manufacturer is easy to hide behind generic furniture or jewelry-retail language. Potential customers may be searching for a showcase, a display cabinet, store fixtures, lighting, security of the equipment, a store layout, or a turnkey salon.

Those queries are related. They are not the same page. The website had to make the manufacturing and installation capability clear without inventing a complaint the source does not record. No historic domain, previous CMS or ranking gap is described, so none is invented.
Two kinds of work sat beside each other for years. Aleks SF designed, engineered, produced and installed jewelry-store equipment. Neolines built and promoted the digital side of that business.

The documented digital scope is keyword and competitor analysis, a semantic core of approximately 1,000 SEO-relevant terms, content architecture on Drupal with HTML, CSS and PHP, SEO-oriented copy, ongoing search promotion, and contextual advertising / paid search. Budgets, ad accounts and a reconstructed historic URL are not disclosed.
