title: NPK BINAR: SEO and Website Development for Complete Roofing Systems
case_study_long_title: NPK BINAR — Semantic SEO and Drupal Website Architecture for Roofing Design, Metal Fabrication, Installation and Drainage Systems

layout.case_study_preview_title: Roofing Design, Manufacturing, and Installation

content.text: NPK BINAR provides integrated roofing solutions, combining roofing-system design, specialist materials and components, installation, and related drainage and building-envelope products. The digital work was a Drupal website with keyword research, competitor analysis, a semantic core and an SEO-oriented structure so those related products and services could be found without collapsing into one generic roofing page. The client relationship lasted approximately two years.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Standing-seam metal roof on a contemporary commercial building, with valleys, ridges and metal flashing.

content.text: NPK BINAR is a roofing and building-envelope business with a broad, interconnected range. The supplied material identifies roofing-system design, roofing installation, copper roofing, zinc roofing, standing-seam roofing, flexible shingles, metal roofing tiles, slate-style products referred to as euroslate, drainage and roof-water management, siding, thermal insulation, and associated roofing materials.

Manufacturing of metal and copper roofing elements and drainage components is part of that picture, together with installation. This record does not claim that every covering in the range was fabricated in-house. It does not call the company an industry leader.

The challenge is not only to rank for a general term such as roofing. Potential customers may search for a material, a roof type, a fabricated flashing, an installation crew, a gutter system, siding, insulation, or a complete roofing solution.

Those queries are related. They are not the same page. The site had to represent the range clearly without creating duplicate or competing URLs. No historic domain, previous CMS or ranking gap is described, so none is invented.

The documented SEO work is keyword research, competitor analysis, development of a semantic core, search-intent mapping, and an information architecture that could hold roofing products, materials, fabricated components and installation services as related categories.

A well-mapped structure can connect a complete-roof page to copper, zinc, standing-seam, tiles, shingles, drainage and installation without making those pages copy each other. No keyword volumes, ranking tables or named competitors are published.
The website was developed on Drupal, with UX/UI design and an SEO-oriented structure. Drupal is the confirmed platform. Version, theme, modules and a reconstructed sitemap are not disclosed.

The practical job of UX/UI here is navigation: help a visitor distinguish roofing materials, roof types, fabricated components and complete installation services. This Case Study describes the historical project, not the current Next.js website.

The range in the source includes copper and zinc roofing, standing-seam systems, metal roofing tiles, flexible shingles, slate-style products named as euroslate, fabricated metal and copper elements, and installation.

The value of the offering is coordination: material selection, component fabrication and installation can sit in one roofing solution. Confirmed fabrication in this record is metal and copper roofing elements and drainage components. Other coverings and envelope products are listed as part of the range; in-house manufacture of those items is not verified.
No product models, material grades or factory capacities are stated.
Gutters, downpipes and other roof-water management products belong with the roof, not beside it. They connect design, fabricated metal details and installation at the eaves.

Siding and thermal insulation are named as complementary building-envelope products. They widen the offering around the roof. They are not reconstructed here as a second facade-contracting business. Models and specifications are not disclosed.

Content marketing and digital promotion are named in the source as project activities. Their intended role is to explain the range — materials, fabricated parts, drainage, installation — and to attract relevant construction and roofing prospects.
No article count, campaign, traffic figure or lead volume is in the source. Those results are not disclosed.

The documented work is a Drupal website with UX/UI design, a semantic SEO foundation and an information architecture for a broad roofing portfolio. The client relationship lasted approximately two years. That figure is the duration of cooperation. It is not reported as a verified SEO-campaign length.

The intended value is structural: buyers can find a material, a fabricated component, a drainage line or an installation service without losing the complete-roof picture. Verified traffic, rankings, leads, conversions and revenue are not in the source. Not disclosed.

layout.case_study_content_title: Lessons for Manufacturing and Construction Businesses

content.text: A broad portfolio fails online when everything is forced onto one roofing homepage. Manufacturers and contractors that combine material supply, fabrication, design, installation and related components need a map: system, material, part, stage.

The transferable lesson is not a Drupal verdict and not a traffic claim. It is the discipline of giving related products their own semantics, then leaving gaps as Not disclosed when the source is silent.

items.question: What are the differences between copper, zinc, standing-seam, and metal-tile roofing?

content.text: These are different materials and system types, which is why they need distinct pages. Copper and zinc are specialist metals with their own detailing. Standing-seam is a long-panel metal system. Metal tiles are a profiled covering that reads as tiles.

title: Ovik Montag: SEO and Website Development for HVAC and Building Engineering Systems
case_study_long_title: Ovik Montag — Semantic SEO and Drupal Website Architecture for HVAC Engineering, Construction Subcontracting and Building-Services Delivery

layout.case_study_preview_title: HVAC Engineering and Installation for Construction Projects

content.text: Ovik Montag is an engineering contractor specializing in heating, ventilation and air-conditioning systems. The offering combines engineering design, installation of building-services systems, production of necessary components where applicable, and ongoing technical maintenance on construction projects. The digital work was a Drupal website with keyword research, competitor analysis, a semantic core and an SEO-oriented structure so those related services could be found without collapsing into a generic montage-company page.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Technicians inspecting ceiling HVAC ductwork inside a commercial building under construction.

content.text: Ovik Montag is an engineering contractor in the construction and building-services sector. The stated service areas are heating systems, ventilation systems, air-conditioning systems, engineering design and planning, installation and integration of building-services systems, production of necessary components and related products where applicable, technical maintenance, and participation in construction projects as an engineering subcontractor.

The company is not described as a generic HVAC repair shop. The useful picture is integrated delivery across stages of a project: design the system, produce or supply needed parts when that applies, install it in the building, then maintain it. This record does not claim that every stage was performed on every job.

A technically broad contractor is easy to flatten online. Heating, ventilation and air conditioning are related, but they are bought as different jobs. Design work, component production, site installation and later servicing also have different search intent.

The challenge was to keep Ovik Montag visible as one engineering contractor working inside construction projects, while still giving each system and each stage a place a technical or construction buyer could land. No historic URL, previous CMS or failed campaign is described, so none is invented. Keyword volumes, competitor brands and ranking gaps are not in the source.

The documented research work is keyword research, competitor analysis, development of a semantic core, and mapping of search intent onto website pages. The job of that map was a coherent information architecture for an engineering contractor: technical service pages that stay related to one another.

A construction buyer looking for ventilation installation on a building should not have to infer it from a paragraph about heating. A facilities buyer looking for maintenance should not land only on a design slogan. A well-organized structure can show the specific HVAC service and still explain the wider capability.
No keyword count, ranking table or competitor list is published. The mapping is the result that can be stated.

The website was developed on Drupal, with UX/UI design and an SEO-oriented information architecture. Drupal is the confirmed platform. Version, theme, modules, integrations and a reconstructed sitemap are not disclosed.

The role of UX/UI here is practical: help a technical visitor move from the contractor picture to the system or stage they need, without a single undifferentiated services page. This Case Study describes the historical project. It is not a description of the current Next.js website.

HVAC projects in this sector commonly involve system components, ductwork and ventilation elements, mounting and connection hardware, equipment, installation, and later servicing. Those are industry examples of what such work can include.

For Ovik Montag, the source supports heating, ventilation and air conditioning as service areas, plus design, installation, maintenance, and production of necessary components where applicable. It does not name a product catalogue, brands, models or a list of manufactured parts. This record does not invent one.

The gallery below illustrates HVAC equipment, ventilation components and building-services installations relevant to the sector. The images are not original photographs of documented Ovik Montag projects.

The documented strategy is search-led: keyword research, competitor analysis, semantic mapping, and a Drupal structure designed so pages could match how construction and engineering buyers search. Content marketing and attracting potential customers are named as project activities.
No article count, publishing calendar, organic-traffic growth, keyword positions, leads, conversion rates or revenue is in the source. Those figures are not disclosed and are not invented.

The documented work is a Drupal website with UX/UI design, a semantic SEO foundation and an information architecture that can hold HVAC systems, project stages and construction-subcontracting context. The intended business value is discoverability: a specialist engineering contractor that can be found for the system and the stage a buyer actually needs.
Verified performance metrics are not in the source. Duration is not stated. The outcome that can be reported is the structure and the research, not a percentage.

layout.case_study_content_title: Lessons for Engineering and Manufacturing Businesses

content.text: Companies that combine engineering, construction subcontracting, component production, installation and maintenance fail online when the website only says they do montage. Buyers search across systems and stages. SEO architecture is how that combination stays visible.

The transferable lesson is not a Drupal verdict and not a traffic claim. It is the discipline of mapping a real multi-stage offering onto pages, then leaving gaps as Not disclosed when the source is silent.

content.text: Security Systems Anhor works with integrated engineering and security systems for commercial buildings, offices, large retail centers and other substantial facilities. The company designs, manufactures, installs and maintains those systems, and the source also names cost estimation and commissioning where a project needs them.

The listed service areas are security and alarm systems; fire detection and fire protection; access control; video surveillance; television systems; telephone systems; computer networks and telecommunications; electrical installation and power supply; electrical lighting; electronic article surveillance and anti-theft systems; and public address and sound systems.

Those are the company’s service areas. This record does not treat them as proof that every system was installed on every object, and it does not name buildings, contracts, equipment models or certifications.

A company with this many related systems has a visibility problem that a slogan cannot fix. Search intent overlaps: security, fire protection, access control, CCTV, networking and electrical engineering are close enough to confuse a thin site, and different enough that one services page will bury most of them.

A generic contractor page can introduce Anhor. It cannot be the page for a fire-detection system, an access-control door, a camera run and a structured-cabling closet at the same time. The digital job was to keep the integrated picture and still make individual services discoverable.

The documented research work is keyword analysis, competitor analysis, a detailed semantic keyword core, and mapping of relevant intent onto the website structure. The aim was a coherent hierarchy of related systems rather than a flat list or a single block of copy.

Useful relationships in that map are system to component, design to installation to maintenance, and building type — office, retail, commercial — where the source supports those audiences. Keyword volumes, competitor brands and ranking tables are not in the source. Not disclosed.

The website was a Drupal project. The source describes SEO-oriented architecture and page mapping, organization of a broad technical service taxonomy, UX/UI improvements and website optimization, with the goal of better organic visibility and a better chance of attracting a relevant audience.

Clear navigation and service landing pages matter here because a technical visitor is looking for a system, not a mood. Drupal version, theme, modules and exact historic URLs are not disclosed. This Case Study is a record of the historical project, not a description of the current Next.js site.

The commercial offer is an integrated security and building-systems contractor: design, production, installation and maintenance across the listed systems. Electrical infrastructure, lighting, telecommunications and anti-theft systems sit in the same family because they belong to the same kind of commercial building, not because every job included every trade.

The documented work is research, semantic mapping, a Drupal website with an SEO-oriented structure, and UX/UI optimization for a company whose catalogue is a set of related building systems.

content.text: A wide engineering portfolio becomes searchable when the website copies the way the work is actually bought: by system, by component, by installation or by maintenance, then linked back to the integrated contractor.

layout.case_study_preview_title: Vimpel Engineering: Digital Positioning for Anechoic Chambers and Electromagnetic Absorbing Solutions

content.text: Vimpel Engineering designed and implemented radio-absorbing materials, wave absorbers and anechoic chambers used to reduce electromagnetic reflections and support measurement in high-tech work. The engagement was not a generic website polish. It combined market and competitor research, semantic architecture, UX/UI, website development and SEO so a specialised engineering offering could be found and understood as solutions, applications and testing requirements rather than as one company page.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Interior of an anechoic chamber with pyramid RF-absorbing panels and an unmarked test fixture.

content.text: Vimpel Engineering was a specialised engineering and manufacturing company working with radio-absorbing materials, electromagnetic absorbers and anechoic chambers. The work sat in environments where reflections must be controlled so equipment and systems can be tested under more predictable conditions.

The historical description names radio electronics, telecommunications and defense systems as relevant fields. This case treats those as application areas the digital structure had to address, not as a list of named programmes or customers.

An anechoic chamber is not a conventional catalogue product. It can involve walls, ceiling, floor, absorbing materials, structure, doors, supporting systems where a project needs them, measurement requirements, installation and site-specific engineering. This record does not claim that Vimpel manufactured every component internally. The working description is an engineering and solution provider responsible for design, development, production and/or installation of specialised systems where the project supported that role.

Maryan Polyak's work was the digital side: research, information architecture, UX/UI, website development, technical content and SEO. The company already had the engineering. The market needed a way to recognise it.
Client: Vimpel Engineering
Industry: Specialised engineering and electromagnetic testing environments
Core solutions: Anechoic chambers, RF and electromagnetic absorbers, wave absorbers, testing environments
Project type: Website design and development, SEO, digital positioning

layout.case_study_content_title: Why This Was a Difficult Project

content.text: The difficulty was not a missing title tag. The product is hard to explain in generic marketing language, and the people who buy it do not share one vocabulary.

A visitor might be an engineer, an R&D team, a laboratory specialist, technical procurement, a telecommunications or electronics manufacturer, an antenna developer, a testing laboratory, or technical management. Aerospace and defense organisations are among the kinds of buyers such environments can serve. This case does not convert that list into confirmed accounts.

The same offering can be searched as an anechoic chamber, an RF absorber, a microwave absorber, an antenna test chamber, an EMC testing chamber, an electromagnetic testing environment or radio-frequency absorbing material. The project therefore required engineering understanding, market research, search research, information architecture, UX/UI, content and SEO together.

Core solutions in the model included anechoic chambers, RF and electromagnetic absorbers, wave absorbers and testing environments. Technical functions included absorption, reduction of reflections, a controlled electromagnetic environment, RF testing, antenna measurement and electromagnetic compatibility testing.

Applications the architecture was designed to address included antenna testing, electronics testing, communication systems, aerospace and aviation electronics, defense systems, radar-related equipment, telecommunications and sensors. Industries in that map included aerospace, defense, telecommunications, electronics, radio engineering, R&D and testing laboratories.

layout.case_study_faq_title: Frequently Asked Questions About Vimpel Engineering

items.question: What is an anechoic chamber in this case?

content.text: Here it means a controlled environment for electromagnetic testing, built so reflections are reduced and measurements can be made with less interference from the room itself. It is an engineered system, not a decorative room. Walls, absorbing materials, access and the testing task belong together. This case does not publish dimensions, frequency ranges or absorption ratings, because they are not in the project record.

items.question: Why does an anechoic chamber need absorbing materials?

content.text: Without absorbing structures, electromagnetic energy reflects from surfaces and distorts the measurement. Absorbers, including wave absorbers, are there to reduce those reflections so the test environment stays controlled. The site had to explain that relationship without turning absorber pages into a substitute for a chamber, or the reverse.

items.question: What types of equipment can be tested in an anechoic chamber?

content.text: The website structure was designed to address testing of antennas, electronic equipment, RF and communication systems, and related high-tech hardware. Radio electronics, telecommunications and defense systems are named in the historical description as relevant fields. Named customers, programmes and pass/fail results are not listed.

items.question: Why was keyword research especially important for Vimpel Engineering?

content.text: The market does not share one vocabulary. Buyers may search for an anechoic chamber, an RF absorber, a microwave absorber, an antenna test chamber or an EMC testing environment. Research was required to connect engineering language with those problem statements before the sitemap was locked.

items.question: How did you structure the website for such a specialized product?

content.text: Around solution, application, industry, technical requirement and engineering response. Chambers, absorbers and testing environments were related layers. Applications such as antenna testing or electronics testing were not dumped onto one Services page. Exact URLs are not reconstructed. Not every cluster became a page.

items.question: What can other engineering companies learn from this project?

content.text: Do not explain a specialised offering on one corporate page. Find how the market names the problem, then build architecture and content that follow that map. Technical understanding without search research leaves the site speaking only to insiders. Search research without engineering understanding produces empty category pages.

content.text: Nesko was a national energy company offering combined work in energy auditing, energy efficiency and the reduction of energy costs. It is not useful to describe it only as an energy company. The commercial object was a solution path: understand consumption, find savings, design a response, select equipment where needed, remove and install hardware when a project required it, and deliver the efficiency project.

The same offering included energy passports and financial instruments used to support and implement efficiency projects. This case does not name subsidy programmes, certificate numbers or specific plants. The working description is a technical energy-services provider for industrial and other large sites.

Maryan Polyak's work sat on the digital side of that offering: market and competitor research, keyword analysis, semantic architecture, service structure, UX, website development, content and SEO. The company did not exist because of marketing. A wide professional offering needed a website that industrial buyers could navigate and search engines could interpret.

Industry: Energy and energy efficiency for industrial and other large facilities

layout.case_study_content_title: Why This Was Not a Simple Corporate Site

content.text: The difficulty was the width of the professional offering, not the lack of a homepage. Nesko had to explain technical services in language a buyer could use, cover a large spread of search intents, separate directions of work, and keep UX and SEO on the same map.

The architecture also had to leave room for later content, including a company blog as part of a long-term search plan. A short corporate site can announce that a company works in energy. It cannot carry audit, passports, optimization, equipment, replacement and implementation as distinct jobs.

The sequence was keyword research, semantic core, search intent, service segmentation, semantic maps, website architecture, content structure, internal linking, then blog and further content. SEO participated in forming the structure. It did not wait for a finished visual design.

The website was the implementation of that research, not a separate visual project. The structure had to hold the main energy-service directions, audit, efficiency, passports, optimization, equipment and its introduction on site, dismantling and installation, informational content and the blog.

Content marketing was required, and the company blog was part of that plan. The blog extended semantic coverage, answered informational queries, explained energy topics, created additional search entry points, supported expert positioning and fed long-term visibility. Article titles from the original engagement are not stored here.

Paid search, social campaigns, email, LinkedIn, PR, CRM and analytics stacks are not listed as completed work. They are not confirmed in the source material used here. Exact keyword volumes, rankings and traffic figures are not published.

layout.case_study_preview_title: PakTradeMash: Search Research and Website Expansion for an Industrial Equipment Supplier

content.text: PakTradeMash worked with packaging equipment and food-production systems: supply, installation, technical implementation and service for industrial buyers, including food-processing businesses. The project expanded and restructured an existing website so search demand for equipment, applications and production solutions could land on relevant pages rather than a limited corporate structure.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Unmarked industrial packaging line with stainless-steel machinery and blank cartons on a conveyor.

content.text: PakTradeMash was a large industrial company working with packaging equipment and production systems. The business was not a retail shopfront. Its customers could include food-production and processing companies that needed equipment and systems for packaging, refrigeration and freezing, food processing, production lines, handling and preparation, and industrial packaging operations.

The company operated across production and manufacturing, equipment supply, installation, technical implementation, maintenance and service, and solutions for food-production businesses. Some equipment or components may have been sourced from other manufacturers while the company also produced or integrated parts of its own solutions. This case does not treat that mix as a verified bill of materials. The working description is a technical industrial supplier and integrator with a broad packaging and food-production equipment offering.

Maryan Polyak's work sat on the digital side of that offering: search research, information architecture, content and SEO. The case is not that the company existed because of marketing. It is that a technically complex catalogue needed a website that industrial buyers could actually find and navigate.

layout.case_study_content_title: The Website Was Too Small for the Offering

content.text: PakTradeMash already had a website and an established industrial business. The digital structure did not fully represent the breadth of equipment, solutions and applications. Promoting the existing pages as they stood would have left most of the catalogue without a corresponding place in search.

The job was to understand how potential industrial buyers searched - packaging equipment and machinery, production lines, refrigeration and freezing equipment, food-production equipment, application-specific kit, related technical solutions - and convert that demand into a logical website structure.
This is a B2B industrial marketing case, not a retail e-commerce story. The buyers are companies looking for equipment, technologies and production solutions, often with long evaluation cycles.

The website was expanded from a relatively limited existing structure into a more comprehensive architecture. The aim was to represent equipment categories, packaging systems, refrigeration and freezing solutions, production lines, applications, food-industry segments, technical information and commercial or service intent.

The architecture connects product, equipment type, application, industry, production need and solution. Industrial SEO here is not adding keywords to the original pages. The structure itself is part of the marketing strategy.
Company / about
Packaging equipment and machinery
Packaging lines and production-line equipment
Refrigeration and freezing solutions
Food-production and processing applications
Meat-processing and vegetable-processing contexts
Installation, implementation and service
Technical information
Contact

These areas follow the supplied project material. Specific URLs are not reconstructed here. Additional equipment types and applications can be added as pages when they match real offering and real search demand, without treating every keyword as a new URL.

The SEO work started with search and competitor research: how industrial buyers name equipment, categories, applications and production processes, and how search results were already organised. Competitor names are not listed, because they are not verified in the current project data. What was used is the pattern: category structure, content gaps, terminology, intent and opportunities for more specific pages.

The semantic core was organised by product, equipment category, application, industry, production process, commercial intent and informational intent. Keywords were mapped to the most relevant pages instead of concentrating every term on the homepage.

Content was created or improved around that demand: equipment, applications and industrial solutions written so a technical buyer could recognise the offering and a search engine could associate the page with the right query. On-page work covered titles, headings, metadata, internal linking, semantic relevance, page structure, content depth and intent alignment.
Exact keyword volumes, ranking positions and traffic figures are not published. They are not verified in the current project data.
The engagement is remembered as a substantial project on the order of a year. That duration is not treated as a verified calendar metric in this record, and the duration field is left empty.

The result that can be stated without inventing figures is qualitative: a broader website structure, stronger semantic coverage, clearer organisation of products and applications, expanded content, and a better foundation for organic search growth in packaging and food-production equipment. Paid campaigns, social programmes and CRM work are not listed as completed channels, because they are not confirmed in the source material used here.

items.question: What was the main SEO challenge with PakTradeMash?

content.text: The company already had a website and an established industrial business. The structure did not fully represent the breadth of equipment, applications and services. The challenge was to understand how industrial buyers searched for packaging, refrigeration, production-line and food-processing solutions, then turn that demand into a logical site architecture rather than chasing traffic on a few general pages.

items.question: Why was keyword research important for an industrial equipment company?

content.text: Buyers rarely search only for the company name. They search for equipment types, production processes and applications: packaging machinery, packaging lines, freezing equipment, food-production equipment. Research showed how those intents were worded so the website could match them with relevant pages instead of one generic corporate description.

items.question: How did you structure search demand across products and applications?

content.text: The semantic core was organised by product, equipment category, application, industry, production process, and commercial versus informational intent. Terms were mapped to the most relevant page type. A packaging-machine query and a meat-processing application query were not forced onto the same URL.

items.question: Why was it not enough to optimize the existing website pages?

content.text: Existing pages can be improved, but they cannot absorb every equipment category and application if the architecture is too small. The project expanded the information architecture so new, relevant pages could exist. SEO here was structural, not only metadata on the original URLs.

items.question: How can an industrial equipment company use content to reach different customer industries?

content.text: By writing to the production problem, not only the product family. Food production, meat processing, vegetable processing and industrial packaging operations describe different jobs. Content that names the application helps a technical buyer recognise the offering. It should still stay within what the company actually supplied and installed.

items.question: What can other manufacturers learn from the PakTradeMash project?

content.text: If the business has many equipment types, applications and customer industries, one general corporate page will not represent it in search. Search research can show how buyers describe those problems. That demand can be translated into architecture, category pages, application pages and useful technical content. The website becomes a structured digital representation of the offering, not only a company presentation.

title: Pnevmomachta — Building a Long-Term Digital Presence for a Technical Mast Manufacturer
case_study_long_title: Pnevmomachta — Website, SEO and Continuous Digital Development for a Pneumatic Mast Manufacturer

layout.case_study_preview_title: Pnevmomachta: More Than Ten Years of Digital Presence for a Focused Mast Manufacturer

content.text: Pnevmomachta designs, engineers and manufactures pneumatic telescopic masts. The engagement with Maryan Polyak has lasted more than ten years. The work was not a one-off website launch. It was the ongoing digital representation of a technically capable manufacturer that had to be findable for the applications its products actually serve.

case_study_preview_image.alt: White portable lighting mast with two LED floodlights on a tripod, outdoors beside a building.

content.text: Pnevmomachta is a manufacturer of pneumatic telescopic masts and related mast equipment. The founder is an engineer and technical developer. The business started from his own understanding that these masts were needed for practical industrial and emergency work, not from reselling a standard catalogue item.

He continues to develop the technical side of the products: mast construction, configurations, applications and equipment. The production range is relatively focused. That is part of the story. A manufacturer does not need thousands of unrelated products to justify a serious digital presence.

Maryan Polyak has worked with this client for more than ten years. The partnership is between engineering, manufacturing, website, SEO, content and continuous development. The case is not that the client became successful because of an agency. It is that a technically capable manufacturer stayed visible as the production itself developed.

The initial challenge was not that the company had no product. The products existed, and the engineering understanding of the market was strong. Potential customers still could not discover the manufacturer simply because the company existed.

Maryan argued that production itself was not enough. The company needed a website that made the manufacturer visible to people already searching for these solutions: what the masts are, where they are used, which configurations exist, and why this manufacturer is the one to contact.

The website therefore became more than an online brochure. It became a long-term digital representation of the production, the products, the engineering expertise and the new developments as they appeared.

layout.case_study_content_title: A Focused Range With Many Applications

content.text: The same core technology can serve different jobs. The source case describes applications including firefighting, construction, lighting, searchlights, antennas, communications, emergency response, special-purpose masts, vehicle-mounted systems and masts for specialized vehicles and services.

That is still one product family. The digital structure has to connect the technical product with the operational problem the buyer is trying to solve, instead of promoting only the generic term “pneumatic mast”.

The site was organized around product types, applications and supporting company information. Relevant areas include company and about, firefighting masts, construction masts, lighting and searchlight masts, antenna masts, communication masts, emergency applications, materials and manufacturing, installation services, turnkey solutions, photo gallery, articles and contact.

The architecture is meant to accept additional configurations without a rebuild. Semantic structure connects product, application, industry, equipment, problem and solution. The goal is not artificial SEO pages. The goal is to explain the actual product ecosystem in the language customers use when they look for a solution.

layout.case_study_content_title: SEO, Content and Photography as Maintenance

content.text: SEO was treated as a long-term process, not a campaign that ended at launch. The work included researching product and application terminology, analysing competitors, identifying commercial intent, building dedicated product and application content, keeping technical SEO in order, and expanding the footprint as real products appeared.
A historic keyword-count from older material is not republished here, because it has not been independently verified in the current project data. The method is what can be stated.

Content follows production. A new mast on a specialized fire vehicle can generate product information, a gallery update, photographs, a technical description, a social post and an internal link from the relevant category. That is a realistic flow. It is not a demand to publish every day.

Photography matters because this is a physical product. Buyers need to see the mast, deployed and collapsed states, mounts, vehicle installations and equipment on the mast. No specific photographs are claimed in this write-up beyond that principle; existing Media items are used only where they already exist in the project.

The website is the central source of structured product and company information. The same material can be adapted for social channels such as LinkedIn and Facebook when a new product or installation is worth showing, with a path back to the technical page.
This case does not claim that every network mentioned in older material is still active, and it does not publish subscriber counts.

Visibility for a manufacturer also includes consistent references in business directories, industry resources, regional listings and maps. Specific directory names are not listed here unless they are already documented in the project.

The relationship was not “build a website and leave”. Over more than ten years the mix included website development, catalogue functionality, SEO, content, product descriptions, new photographs, galleries, social support, advertising when appropriate, analytics and ongoing technical improvements. The combination changed. The principle did not: the website should continue to reflect the real production.

The result that can be stated without inventing figures is qualitative. The site has remained discoverable for years and continues to generate visibility and inquiries for a specialized manufacturer. The digital presence is an accumulated asset rather than a short campaign.

items.question: What exactly does Pnevmomachta manufacture?

content.text: Pnevmomachta specializes in pneumatic telescopic mast systems and related configurations for applications including firefighting, construction, lighting, antennas, communications and emergency response.

items.question: Why does a specialized manufacturer need such a large digital presence?

content.text: Even a focused product range can serve many different applications. Customers may search for a mast for a specific vehicle, lighting system, firefighting application, antenna or construction task rather than searching only for the general product name. A structured website allows the manufacturer to be found through these different requirements.

items.question: How can a manufacturer keep its website current without publishing news every day?

content.text: It does not need to publish artificial daily news. Real production activity is enough. New products, configurations, installations, photographs and technical information can be added when they actually exist.

items.question: Why are photographs important for technical manufacturing products?

content.text: Technical buyers want to understand how a product looks and how it is used. Photographs of real products, installations and configurations provide evidence of the manufacturer’s actual capabilities and help visitors understand the application.

items.question: Does SEO for a manufacturing company end after the website is built?

content.text: No. A strong initial structure provides the foundation, but ongoing additions of real products, applications, technical content, photographs and internal links allow the website to continue developing its search visibility over time.

items.question: Can the same product content be used on social media?

content.text: Yes, with appropriate adaptation. A new product or installation can become website content, a gallery update and social media content. The website remains the deeper source of technical information while social channels help distribute and expose that information to additional audiences.

content.text: The problem was not the number of products. The problem was that the right customer had to be able to find the manufacturer when a specific need appeared. A specialized product can have many applications, and each application creates a different search intent.

A visitor looking for a firefighting mast, a lighting mast for a construction site, or an antenna mast for a vehicle is not looking for a generic company page. If those applications are not explained, the manufacturer stays invisible even though the product exists.

And when those photographs are connected to the correct product and application pages, they become part of the information architecture.
A gallery that is not tied to those pages is decoration. A gallery that is tied to them is evidence.

One generic “pneumatic mast” page cannot carry those intents. Dedicated application content can, because each page answers a search the buyer actually types.

A firefighting mast is still a mast, and it is also an emergency application. Internal links make that relationship visible instead of forcing the visitor to guess.
New configurations can be added as new pages without rebuilding the tree, which is what a ten-year site actually needs.

Linking them keeps the engineering accurate and still lets each industry arrive through its own language.

The stronger asset here is that a specialized buyer can still find and understand the manufacturer years after the first website work, because the site continued to reflect real production rather than a launch-day snapshot.

The same principle applies where Facebook is an appropriate channel for the audience. No subscriber count or current activity claim is published.
Photographs of real installations are more useful here than generic company news, again linking back to the website when the visitor needs specifications.

Over more than ten years the site accumulates structured information about the company, products, applications and expertise: technical descriptions, application pages, photographs and updates that follow real production.

No claim is made that ChatGPT, Gemini or another AI system ranked the company. There is no verified AI-search measurement in this case. The statement is architectural: there is more accurate material for a system to read than there would be from a one-page brochure that never changed.

The semantic structure treats the manufacturer, the mast technology and the applications as related entities rather than a single generic product keyword. Firefighting, lighting, antennas, communications and vehicle mounts are distinct uses of the same capability.
That is information architecture. It is not a measured GEO or AEO programme, and none is claimed.

Confirmed shape of the work, without inventing a dated project plan: understand the products and applications with the engineer-client; build a website structured around those applications; establish SEO and content around real search intent; keep photography and galleries tied to products; reuse material on social channels when there is something real to show; maintain consistent company references in listings and maps; continue the work as production develops.
Advertising was used when appropriate. It was not the model. The engagement is measured in more than ten years, not in a launch sprint.

A site structured around products, applications and company information, so a searching buyer could understand the masts and make contact. Exact calendar years for the first launch are not restated here beyond the verified length of the relationship: more than ten years.

New configurations, photographs, technical descriptions and application pages added as they existed. SEO, internal linking and channel reuse continued. The mix of website, content, social support and advertising shifted; the requirement that the site reflect real production did not.

A focused manufacturing business became continuously visible online through long-term digital work. The value was not simply the creation of an online store. The real result was the creation and maintenance of a digital representation of a technical manufacturer that could grow with the production.

As new products, configurations, photographs and applications appeared, they could be added to the website and distributed through other channels. That created a cumulative digital presence that continued working long after the initial website development.

The website has remained discoverable in search for years and continues to generate visibility and inquiries for a specialized manufacturer. Verified current commercial figures are not stored in this project, so none are published.
Maryan Polyak has worked with Pnevmomachta for more than ten years. The duration is the verified result. It is not a traffic percentage.

The production range is relatively focused. The digital structure still covers distinct applications such as firefighting, construction, lighting, antennas, communications and emergency response, because those are how buyers search.

Application content for firefighting, emergency response and specialized service vehicles, where rapid deployment and elevated equipment matter. No individual installation is named here beyond the application itself.
Mast systems presented as part of construction-site and temporary lighting applications, using product information and installation examples rather than a generic product-only page.
Configurations for antennas, communication equipment and specialized vehicles, treated as their own content opportunities when a new mount or installation appears.

A manufacturing website does not need to look busy every day to be valuable. A factory may develop one important product configuration this month and have nothing genuinely newsworthy to publish tomorrow. That is normal.

The important thing is to make sure that real production activity is reflected online. A new product, a new mounting system, a new vehicle installation, a new photograph or a new technical application can become useful digital information.
Over ten years, these small updates accumulate. The result is not just a website. It is a growing digital record of what the manufacturer actually does.

For a specialized manufacturer, that accumulated record can become more valuable than a short advertising campaign because it remains discoverable and continues to provide context for future customers.
More than ten years of website, SEO and content work for a pneumatic mast manufacturer, kept in step with real production rather than treated as a one-off launch.

title: Laser Made: From a Broken Landing Page to Two Working Manufacturing Websites
case_study_long_title: Laser Made: How a Full-Cycle Laser Cutting and Furniture Manufacturer Replaced Two Unstructured Landing Pages With Two Purpose-Built Websites and Five Years of Continuous Digital Growth

layout.case_study_preview_title: Laser Made: Five Years, Two Websites, One System That Still Works

content.text: Laser Made is a full-cycle production company working with wood, acrylic, MDF and metal. In 2019 the business had two slow, unstructured WordPress landing pages and no clear way for visitors to understand what it actually made. Over five years the site was rebuilt on Drupal, split into a B2B corporate platform and a B2C decor store, and supported by SEO, PPC, content and social media working together.

case_study_preview_image.alt: Laser Made: How a Full-Cycle Laser Cutting and Furniture Manufacturer Replaced Two Unstructured Landing Pages

content.text: Laser Made is a full-cycle manufacturing company. Its own production facilities handle laser cutting, milling, painting and assembly, run by an in-house team of specialists. Materials worked on include wood, acrylic, MDF and metal. Output ranges from custom furniture and decorative items to advertising structures and souvenirs.
Before the project, the company had the equipment and the production capacity, but almost no visibility online.

The company ran on two WordPress landing pages. Both were slow and had no real structure. Design, production, equipment and services were all crammed onto the same page, so a visitor had no clear way to tell what the company actually did.

There was no portfolio and no case studies, only a plain list of services. SEO was effectively absent. Paid search spend was going nowhere. Social media accounts existed but were run without a plan and produced no measurable result.

content.text: The WordPress landing pages were retired and the site was rebuilt on Drupal. The new structure was organized around the actual production process rather than a generic services list:
Material processing, 15 categories (plywood, wood, MDF, composite, acrylic, PVC, plastic, and others)
Outdoor advertising, 7 sections, from illuminated letters to roof-mounted installations
Interior advertising: exhibition equipment, wayfinding signage, retail space fit-out
POS materials and retail equipment
Screens, stained-glass elements, custom furniture, partitions
A portfolio section with 200+ documented projects, a press and blog center, and a dedicated client-resources section

A second, separate storefront, Decor Trend, was launched for retail decor sales. It runs as its own platform with its own audience and promotion approach: the corporate site (Laser Made) serves B2B, the store serves B2C.

The semantic core behind the new structure covers 2,000+ keywords, broken down by individual material, process and application (for example, distinguishing "MDF milling" from generic "laser cutting" queries).
New site built on Drupal from the ground up
15 material-processing categories defined: plywood, wood, MDF, acrylic, plastic, PVC, composite, polycarbonate, PET, paper, cardboard, felt, fabric, leather, rubber
7 outdoor-advertising sections defined: letters, boxes and lightboxes, signs, plaques, stands, large structures, entrance groups
Interior advertising, POS materials and retail-equipment sections built out
Semantic core collected and clustered (2,000+ queries)
Baseline PPC campaigns launched for early traffic
Analytics and conversion tracking configured
Optimized content written for each service and material category
Portfolio populated with 200+ real projects
Blog launched with expert articles, typically built from a 30-minute interview with the client turned into a roughly 2,000-word article
Decor Trend online store developed and launched
Link building through industry publications, mixing free guest posts on industry blogs with paid placements in directories and design and construction media
10+ social media channels actively managed, including VKontakte, YouTube, Odnoklassniki, Telegram, Pinterest, Twitter/X and Instagram, covering content planning, shooting and design
Jivo live chat integrated for instant client contact

layout.case_study_faq_title: Frequently Asked Questions About Laser Made

items.question: How do you structure a site for a workshop that processes 15 different materials without turning navigation into an unusable list?

content.text: The structure follows the production process, not a services menu. The 27+ sections on the corporate site are grouped into six practical areas: material processing, outdoor advertising, interior advertising, POS and retail equipment, screens and furniture and decor, and a press-center plus client-resources area.

Within material processing the 15 categories exist as their own destinations — plywood, wood, MDF, acrylic, plastic, PVC, composite, polycarbonate, PET, paper, cardboard, felt, fabric, leather and rubber. That matters because a buyer does not search for "laser cutting", they search for the material they hold in their hand. A single generic services page cannot answer that, and it also cannot rank for it.

items.question: Why split the business across two websites instead of adding a shop section to the corporate site?

content.text: Because the two audiences buy differently. The corporate site serves B2B clients commissioning custom production: they need technical detail, material and process specifics, and evidence of comparable work. The separate store serves B2C buyers of finished decor items, where the decision is short and visual.

Merging them re-creates the original problem in a new form — one page trying to speak to everyone, which is exactly what made the 2019 landing pages unreadable. Keeping them apart lets each platform have its own audience, content and promotion approach.

items.question: What does a 2,000+ keyword semantic core actually buy a manufacturer?

content.text: It buys specificity. The core is clustered by individual material, process and application rather than a small set of head terms, so "MDF milling" is treated as distinct from generic "laser cutting" demand. Each cluster then has a page that genuinely answers it.

The compounding effect showed up late: by years four and five, hundreds of keywords had reached top positions in Google. That is the honest shape of the result — not a step change after launch, but breadth accumulating over years as content matched what the workshop actually produces.

items.question: Where did qualified B2B enquiries actually come from?

content.text: Several routes, deliberately matched to intent. A short name-and-phone form on the homepage captures fast enquiries. An extended form on service pages asks for service type, material and timeline, which qualifies the lead before anyone picks up the phone. A price calculator turns material and size into an estimate. Live chat accounts for roughly 15 to 20% of leads, on the condition that chats are answered within one to two minutes. WhatsApp and Telegram are offered as direct channels.

On channel mix, the source data gives an approximate split of about 50% from Google Ads, 30% from organic search, 15% from social media and 5% direct. That is presented as an estimate rather than an audited figure, and it is worth treating it as one.

items.question: Does this kind of structure help with AI and generative search visibility?

content.text: Honest answer: no measured AI-search results are claimed for this project. What exists is the groundwork that AI answers tend to draw on — a structure that ties material to the processes performed on it and to the finished product categories that use it, a 200+ project portfolio, an expert blog built from client interviews, a project FAQ, and Google My Business reviews.

That is standard information-architecture and authority work rather than a dedicated generative-search programme. It positions the business to be described accurately by a system that reads structure, but claiming measured visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity or Gemini for this engagement would be inventing a result.

comments.author: Daniel Hoffman
comments.role: Industrial marketing consultant

content.text: The part I keep coming back to is the 15 material categories. Most fabricators I work with have the same breadth and they all end up with one "our services" page because nobody can agree how to divide it. How did you actually decide the six top-level groups rather than, say, splitting by machine?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: Splitting by machine is the trap, because it describes the workshop to itself rather than to a buyer. Nobody commissions "the CNC router". The six groups follow what the output is for: material processing, outdoor advertising, interior advertising, POS and retail equipment, screens and furniture and decor, and the client-resources area.

Material is the entry point because it is the one thing a buyer already knows before they know anything else. Process lives underneath it, which is why 3D milling and CNC facade work sit inside material processing rather than as peers of it.

comments.author: Petra Lindqvist
comments.role: Technical SEO lead

content.text: 2,000+ keywords across 27+ sections raises the obvious question: how did you avoid producing a field of thin near-duplicate pages? Material-by-material pages are notoriously easy to turn into doorway content.

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: The clustering is what prevents it. A cluster only becomes a page if it has something specific to say — a material with its own tolerances, thicknesses, finishes and typical applications. Where two clusters would say the same thing, they belong on one page with the second as a section, not as a separate URL.

The other half is content that is not templated. Each service and material category got written content rather than a generated variant, and the portfolio carries 200+ documented projects that give those categories real examples to point at. A page with a real project on it is very hard to mistake for a doorway.

comments.author: Petra Lindqvist
comments.role: Technical SEO lead

content.text: And cannibalisation between the material pages and the process pages? "MDF" and "MDF milling" are close enough to compete.

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: They are, and the resolution is hierarchy rather than keyword avoidance. The material page owns the material as a whole and links down; the process page owns the specific operation and links up. One is the category, one is the answer to a narrower query. Problems appear when both pages try to be the category — then you are competing with yourself and Google picks for you.

comments.author: Ruben Castellanos
comments.role: Web development studio owner

content.text: Curious about the platform decision. Moving off WordPress to Drupal in 2019 for a fabrication business — what made that the right call rather than rebuilding on WordPress properly?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: The deciding factor was the structure itself. What had to be modelled was a taxonomy with real depth — materials, processes, applications and product categories that cross-reference each other — plus a portfolio that had to grow past 200 entries and stay navigable.

I would not present that as a universal verdict on the two platforms. The honest version is that the site was rebuilt from the ground up on Drupal and the structure held for five years without needing another rebuild, which is the outcome that actually mattered.

comments.author: Ilana Fischer
comments.role: B2B demand generation

content.text: You describe two form types — a short one on the homepage and an extended one on service pages. In practice, did the longer form suppress volume? That is usually the objection from sales.

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: It changes what you are optimising for. The short form exists precisely because some visitors will not fill in anything longer, so it stays as the low-friction route. The extended form asks for service type, material and timeline, and its job is qualification — those three answers tell you whether an enquiry is a real project before anyone spends time on it.
For custom production that trade is usually worth it, because the cost of an unqualified enquiry is a quote that takes real engineering time to prepare.

comments.author: Ilana Fischer
comments.role: B2B demand generation

content.text: Where does the price calculator sit in that? I would expect a fabricator to resist publishing anything that looks like a price.

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: It gives an estimate from material and size, not a quote, and that distinction is what makes it acceptable. Its real function is filtering: a visitor who sees the rough order of magnitude and continues is a different prospect from one who had no idea. It removes the conversation that ends at the number.

comments.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
comments.role: PPC specialist, industrial accounts

content.text: On the paid side — you mention an A/B test where a price-free emotional headline beat a price-led one by around 20% on CTR and conversion. Did that hold for the B2B production campaigns, or mainly the consumer decor side?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: I would not stretch that result further than it goes. It is one documented headline test, and the roughly 20% improvement applies to that test rather than to the account as a whole. Treating it as a rule about B2B versus B2C would be overreading a single comparison.

What is safe to generalise is the practice, not the finding: continuous A/B testing of headlines, images, descriptions and landing pages, with tighter audience targeting used to bring cost per click down over time. The starting point was paid search that was spending without direction, so the gain came from testing at all.

comments.author: Tomasz Wierzbicki
comments.role: PPC specialist, industrial accounts

content.text: Fair. Did the segmented site structure change what you could do in the ad account?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: Significantly, and this is the part that gets missed. Ad groups can only be as specific as the page they land on. With one generic services page every keyword lands in the same place, so match quality is capped no matter how well the account is built. Once each material and process has a real destination, the campaign can mirror the structure instead of fighting it.

comments.author: Noa Berger
comments.role: Export manager, metal fabrication

content.text: We are looking at a similar rebuild but with three languages from the start. Did this project run multilingual, and would you sequence it differently knowing what you know?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: This engagement was single-language, so I cannot offer you measured results from it on the multilingual side. I would rather say that plainly than generalise from a project that did not test it.

What does transfer is the sequencing risk. The expensive mistake here would be translating a structure you are not yet sure about. The material, process and application hierarchy took real work to get right, and every language multiplies the cost of changing it later. Settling the architecture in one language first is the cheaper order of operations.

comments.author: Marek Doležal
comments.role: Content strategist

content.text: The blog model interests me — roughly a 30-minute client interview turned into a ~2,000-word article. How do you keep that going for years without the client losing patience with it?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: By keeping their side of it to the 30 minutes. The interview is the only thing that needs the client, because it is the only part that cannot be sourced elsewhere — how they actually solved a specific job. Writing, editing and publishing do not involve them.

The cadence was front-loaded: 10 to 15 foundational articles first, then 2 to 4 a month. That ordering matters, because the foundational set is what the category pages link into. Starting with a monthly drip leaves the structure with nothing to support it.

comments.author: Marek Doležal
comments.role: Content strategist

content.text: Did the interview-led articles do anything for trust beyond search traffic?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: That is arguably their main job. A buyer commissioning custom production is trying to establish competence before they make contact, and an article that explains how a specific problem was solved does that better than a capability list. Together with the portfolio and the project FAQ, it means the case for the company is already made before the first call.

comments.author: Grace Oyelaran
comments.role: Frontend performance engineer

content.text: The original landing pages are described as slow. Where did the rebuilt site land on performance, and how much of that was structural versus asset-level work?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: The figures recorded for this project are roughly 1.5 to 2 seconds on desktop, 2.5 to 3 seconds on mobile, and a Google PageSpeed score in the 85 to 90 range. For a portfolio-heavy manufacturing site that is a reasonable place to be.

Most of it is asset-level — a site showing 200+ documented projects lives and dies by image handling. But some is structural: when a visitor can reach the specific material they came for in one step, they load one relevant page instead of hunting through a page that carries everything.

comments.author: Sven Aaltonen
comments.role: Head of digital, contract manufacturing

content.text: Everyone is now asking whether their site is "AI-search ready". Given this structure, do you see evidence that it helps in generative answers, or is that still speculation?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: For this project it is speculation, and I will not dress it up. Nothing in the engagement measured visibility in AI answer engines, so there is no result to report.

What I will say is that the work that makes a site legible to an AI system is not a separate discipline. Explicit entities, a material linked to the processes performed on it and to the product categories that use it, a clear split between the B2B production business and the B2C store, documented projects, reviews — that is the same information architecture and authority work you would do anyway. If generative search rewards it, this site is positioned for it. That is a different sentence from claiming it already has.

comments.author: Adela Marchetti
comments.role: Marketing director, furniture manufacturing

content.text: What stands out is the five years rather than any single number. Most agencies would have presented this as a redesign case. Was the long engagement a deliberate model or just how it turned out?

comments.author: Maryan Polyak
comments.role: Manufacturing Digital Marketing & Web Development Expert

content.text: It is the finding, not the framing. A catalogue this wide is not fixed by a redesign, because the work is keeping content and campaigns matched to what the workshop can actually produce — and that changes. The five years cover a Drupal rebuild, the semantic core, the portfolio, a second platform for retail, 10+ social channels, then years of testing and automation from enquiry through to production.

I would rather present that than a growth percentage. Manufacturers are, in my experience, the audience least impressed by a chart and most interested in whether something is still working after year three.

company_logo.alt: Laser Made company logo

content.text: Laser Made operates its own production facilities with an in-house team. Confirmed operations include laser cutting, milling (including 3D milling and CNC facade work), painting and assembly. The source data describes this as a full production cycle rather than a single isolated process.

Custom furniture (wardrobes, kitchens, bar counters, wine cellars), decorative screens and partitions, interior wall panels, outdoor advertising structures (illuminated letters, lightboxes, signs, plaques, stands, pylons and roof installations), POS and retail equipment (bar counters, glass display cases, retail shelving), and decor items such as radiator screens and stained-glass elements. Souvenir products are also mentioned in the general description.

Wood, acrylic, MDF and metal are named directly in the source description. The expanded material-processing structure built into the site adds plywood, plastic, PVC, composite, polycarbonate, PET, paper, cardboard, felt, fabric, leather and rubber, 15 categories in total.

A visitor could not tell what the company actually did. There was no portfolio or case-study material to build trust. Paid search spend was not producing results, and social media activity had no defined strategy or measurable outcome. SEO was effectively not being done.

Give the business a digital structure that clearly separates the B2B production offering from a B2C retail line, build organic visibility for the specific materials and processes the company actually performs, and turn paid advertising and portfolio content into a working lead source. No fixed numeric KPIs are stated in the source data for the start of the project.

The corporate site covers the core production business: material processing, outdoor and interior advertising, POS and retail equipment, and custom furniture and decor manufactured to order. The audience is other businesses commissioning custom production work.

Structure and content organized around the specific material, process and application (2,000+ keyword semantic core), supported by a 200+ project portfolio and PPC campaigns targeting commercial buyers.
A separate online store selling finished home-decor products to individual consumers, run as its own platform apart from the production-focused corporate site.

Positioned and promoted independently from the corporate site, as its own storefront with its own audience. The source data does not detail channel-by-channel tactics specific to this store beyond its separate launch and positioning.

Two Drupal-built websites (Laser Made, Decor Trend), Jivo live chat for on-site messaging, Google My Business for local search presence and reviews, and Google Ads for paid search. Contact routes include WhatsApp and Telegram alongside on-site forms.

Laser Made: 27+ sections built around 15 material-processing categories, 7 outdoor-advertising sections, interior advertising, POS and retail equipment, screens, furniture and decor, and a press-center and client-resources area.
Decor Trend: a standalone e-commerce structure for finished decor products. The specific sub-page breakdown is not detailed in the source data.

Semantic research and keyword clustering (2,000+ queries), content written per service and material, a blog built from client interviews (roughly 30 minutes of interview per 2,000-word article, starting with 10 to 15 foundational articles then 2 to 4 per month), a 200+ project portfolio, technical performance work (desktop load time 1.5 to 2s, mobile 2.5 to 3s, Google PageSpeed score 85 to 90), link building combining free guest posts with paid placements in industry directories and media, and Google My Business setup for local SEO.

A price calculator (material and size to estimated price) is also available. Jivo live chat accounts for roughly 15 to 20% of leads, on the condition that chats are answered within 1 to 2 minutes. WhatsApp and Telegram are offered as direct contact channels.
Continuous PPC campaigns aimed at both the B2B production audience and B2C decor buyers, with precise audience targeting used to bring down cost per click.

Ongoing A/B testing of headlines, images, descriptions and landing pages. One documented test compared a price-led headline against an emotional, price-free headline. The emotional version outperformed on both CTR and conversion by roughly 20%.

Per one comment on the source page, Google Ads accounts for roughly 50% of leads, versus about 30% from organic search, 15% from social media and 5% from direct traffic. This breakdown is presented as an approximate estimate in the source, not an audited figure.

Content shows production processes and finished projects rather than direct advertising.
Used for video content covering production processes, project case examples and reviews, expanded in years 4 and 5.

Covers the remaining channels named in the source data: VKontakte, Odnoklassniki, Pinterest and Twitter/X, run as part of the same 10+ channel content plan. Aggregate result confirmed in the source is 10+ active channels with regular publications, with no per-channel performance metrics given.

Trust signals confirmed in the source data: a 200+ project portfolio, an expert blog built on client interviews, a 13-question project FAQ, and Google My Business reviews (rating cited as 4.5 to 5 stars). No claims are made in the source data about results in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or other AI search engines, and none are implied here.

The site existing structure ties material, process and application together, for example linking a specific material category to the processes performed on it and the finished-product categories that use it, and separates the business into B2B production and B2C retail. This is standard SEO and information-architecture work. The source data does not describe a dedicated GEO or AEO program, so none is claimed here.

Confirmed stages, drawn from both the main narrative and the FAQ: audit of the starting situation, competitor review (checking the Google top 10 for relevant queries), semantic research and clustering, migration from WordPress to Drupal, architecture and content build-out, PPC launch, analytics and conversion-tracking setup, and ongoing optimization (A/B testing, CPC reduction, content and channel expansion, workflow automation).

A/B testing, CPC reduction, keywords reaching Google top positions, video content, request-to-production automation.

Starting from two unstructured WordPress landing pages with no clear positioning, the project produced two purpose-built websites: a B2B corporate platform with 27+ organized sections and a separate B2C decor store. This was backed by a 2,000+ keyword semantic core, a 200+ project portfolio, and 10+ actively managed social channels.

The company became findable for hundreds of relevant search queries, and paid campaigns moved from an undirected budget drain to a continuously tested, targeted channel. The five-year continuous engagement is itself presented in the source data as the primary evidence that the system kept producing value rather than a one-time fix.

content.text: Custom-made wooden bar countertop designed for a residential or commercial interior. The countertop combines natural wood with a clean, functional design and is manufactured to fit the specific dimensions and layout of the space. Its solid construction and carefully finished surface provide both durability for everyday use and a refined architectural element within the interior.

The core production challenge here was breadth, not depth. One workshop makes furniture, outdoor advertising, interior fit-out, POS equipment and decor, using 15 different materials. A single generic "laser cutting services" page cannot carry that. The site had to be organized the way the workshop actually works, material by material and process by process, or visitors and search engines would default back to a shallow, generic read of the business.

Splitting production (B2B) from decor retail (B2C) into two separate platforms matters for the same reason a factory floor is separated from a showroom: the buyers, the content, and the sales cycle are different, and merging them back into one site would have re-created the original clarity problem in a new form.

The five-year duration is itself the more instructive data point for other manufacturing businesses. A catalog this wide is not fixed by a single redesign, it is maintained through years of matching content and campaigns to what the workshop is actually capable of producing.
Five years of structured digital work turned two broken WordPress landing pages into two working websites: one for B2B production clients, one for retail decor buyers.
